Nutrition & Dietary Guidelines

Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 — the inverted food pyramid, with protein, dairy, and healthy fats on top. Click to read the framework.

Core Framework & Principles

Issued January 7, 2026 by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). The 10-page guidelines bring back the food pyramid — flipped upside down, replacing MyPlate as the federal nutrition icon — with protein, dairy, and healthy fats at the top.

Protein, Dairy & Healthy Fats

Top tier: red meat, eggs, whole milk, yogurt, butter.

1.2–1.6 g/kg/day (0.55–0.73 g/lb/day)
Vegetables & Fruits

Middle tier: whole vegetables and fruit every day.

3 veg · 2 fruit / day
Whole Grains

Bottom tier: whole wheat bread, rice, oats.

2–4 servings / day

Also emphasized: whole foods first, a sharp cut in ultra-processed foods, and stricter limits on added sugars.

Evidence-Informed Cooking & Nutrition Tips

68 evidence-informed tips — click to browse them all. The same tips are also linked from inside the recipes where they apply.

From the Evidence-Informed Nutrition and Cooking Guide — themes drawn from the work of Rhonda Patrick, Peter Attia, Andrew Huberman, and Jo Robinson (Eating on the Wild Side), plus mainstream dietary research. Not medical advice.

How to read the evidence tags: [Strong] Supported by large trials or consistent long-term evidence. [Moderate] Reasonable human evidence, but smaller or less consistent. [Limited] Mostly lab, mechanistic, or small-study evidence. Low risk, uncertain payoff.

Two things to keep in mind: changes in nutrient absorption or biomarkers don’t automatically mean fewer diseases or a longer life — and overall dietary pattern matters far more than any single food or trick.

Top 10: Start Here (10 tips)
  1. Eat plenty of fiber, aiming for 30 g or more per day from vegetables, legumes, fruit, whole grains, nuts, and seeds. [Strong]
  2. Make extra virgin olive oil your main everyday fat. [Strong]
  3. Eat legumes (lentils, beans, chickpeas) several times a week. [Strong]
  4. Eat fatty fish (salmon, sardines, trout, herring) twice a week. [Strong]
  5. Get enough protein (roughly 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg (0.55 to 0.73 g/lb) body weight for most active adults), spread across 3 to 4 meals. [Moderate to Strong]
  6. Minimize ultra-processed foods, added sugar, and excess sodium. [Strong]
  7. Eat cruciferous vegetables regularly, and chop them ahead of cooking. [Moderate]
  8. Eat a variety of colorful fruits and vegetables, fresh or frozen. [Strong]
  9. Walk 10 to 15 minutes after meals when you can. [Moderate]
  10. Limit alcohol. Less is better. [Strong]
1. Get More From Plant Compounds (5 tips)
  1. Chop and rest. Chop or crush broccoli, garlic, and onions, then wait about 10 minutes for garlic and onions and 30 to 40 minutes for broccoli before cooking. This lets enzymes (myrosinase in cruciferous vegetables, alliinase in garlic) form protective compounds such as sulforaphane and allicin before heat deactivates them. [Limited to Moderate]
  2. Eat broccoli sprouts. They are very rich in glucoraphanin, the precursor to sulforaphane, which activates the Nrf2 antioxidant-response pathway. Add them raw to salads, eggs, sandwiches, and lentils. [Limited to Moderate]
  3. Add mustard powder to cooked crucifers. If broccoli has been cooked (which destroys myrosinase), about ½ to 1 teaspoon of mustard powder restores enzyme activity. It isn’t needed for raw broccoli. [Limited]
  4. Eat purple and deeply colored produce. Red cabbage, blueberries, blackberries, purple carrots, and purple potatoes contain anthocyanins, which are associated with vascular and metabolic health. [Moderate]
  5. Include onions regularly. They provide quercetin and sulfur compounds. Eat them raw in salads or gently cooked in soups, beans, and lentils. [Limited to Moderate]
2. Choose and Store Produce Well (7 tips)
  1. Favor darker, more colorful varieties. Red leaf lettuce, dark cherries, berries, and smaller tomatoes often contain more anthocyanins and other polyphenols than pale or large varieties. [Limited]
  2. Tearing lettuce may help. Some research suggests that damaging leaves ahead of time can raise certain antioxidants. The evidence is thin, so treat it as optional. [Limited]
  3. Eat delicate produce sooner. Spinach, asparagus, and broccoli lose nutrients during storage, so buy smaller amounts more often. [Moderate]
  4. Store tomatoes at room temperature until ripe. Refrigeration dulls flavor and texture. Refrigerate once ripe if you need more time.
  5. Store potatoes cool and dark, not refrigerated. Cold can convert starch to sugar, changing flavor and cooking behavior. Avoid sunlight, which causes greening.
  6. Buy frozen produce freely. Frozen vegetables and berries are picked and frozen at peak ripeness and can be nutritionally equal or better than “fresh” that has traveled for days. [Strong]
  7. Wash produce under running water, before cutting. Don’t use soap or detergents.
3. Cook to Improve Nutrient Availability (9 tips)
  1. Cook tomatoes and carrots. Heat softens cell walls and increases availability of lycopene and beta-carotene. [Moderate]
  2. Pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients. Olive oil, avocado, nuts, eggs, or butter improve absorption of carotenoids and vitamins A, D, E, and K from tomatoes, carrots, and leafy greens. Finish vegetables with a drizzle of extra virgin olive oil. [Moderate]
  3. Cook spinach lightly. It cooks down so you can eat more. Boiling and then discarding the water reduces oxalates (relevant for people prone to kidney stones). Cooking alone doesn’t solve this. [Moderate]
  4. Steam cruciferous vegetables briefly. Short steaming (a few minutes) preserves more beneficial compounds than prolonged boiling. [Moderate]
  5. Roast or steam beets. They contain betalains and dietary nitrates and are easier to eat cooked.
  6. Cook, cool, and reheat potatoes. Cooling creates some resistant starch, which may modestly improve glucose responses and feed gut bacteria. The effect is real but modest, and reheating retains part of it. [Limited to Moderate]
  7. Soak and thoroughly cook beans and legumes. This reduces antinutritional factors, improves digestibility, and lowers gas-producing oligosaccharides. Dried kidney beans must be boiled thoroughly, as undercooked ones are toxic. [Moderate]
  8. Use cooking liquids. Nutrients that leach into water stay in soups, sauces, and stews.
  9. Vary your cooking methods. Rotate steaming, roasting, sautéing, pressure cooking, and raw preparation. Raw isn’t always healthier. Some nutrients are better preserved with minimal heat, others become more available with cooking.
4. Build a Healthier Gut Microbiome (3 tips)
  1. Eat a variety of fibers. Different bacteria use different fibers, so rotate oats, legumes, berries, vegetables, seeds, and whole grains. [Strong]
  2. Eat lentils, beans, and other resistant-starch foods often. Legumes, green bananas, and cooled potatoes or rice supply fermentable carbohydrates that support short-chain fatty acid production. [Moderate to Strong]
  3. Include fermented foods. Plain kefir, plain yogurt, kimchi, and sauerkraut provide live microbes. Choose refrigerated, unpasteurized versions with live cultures. Early research links fermented food intake with greater microbiome diversity and lower inflammation markers. [Moderate]
5. Cardiovascular and Metabolic Health (7 tips)
  1. Eat fatty fish at least twice a week. Sardines, salmon, trout, and herring provide EPA and DHA omega-3s. [Strong]
  2. Eat a variety of nuts and seeds. Walnuts, almonds, pumpkin seeds, chia, and flax supply healthy fats, fiber, minerals, and polyphenols. [Strong]
  3. Use extra virgin olive oil as your main cooking fat. It is a core component of Mediterranean-style eating. For high-heat cooking, it is more stable than commonly believed, but avoid smoking it. [Strong]
  4. Use vinegar with carb-heavy meals. Acetic acid may modestly lower post-meal glucose. Put balsamic or red wine vinegar in dressings. Don’t drink concentrated vinegar. The evidence comes from small, short studies. [Limited]
  5. Eat vegetables and protein before starches. This sequence can reduce post-meal glucose spikes. Evidence is mostly from small trials, largely in people with diabetes or prediabetes. [Limited to Moderate]
  6. Walk 10 to 15 minutes after meals. Working muscles take up glucose, blunting post-meal spikes. [Moderate]
  7. Minimize ultra-processed foods. Build meals around whole or minimally processed foods with recognizable ingredients, fiber, protein, and little added sugar. [Strong]
6. Protein, Muscle, and Recovery (6 tips)
  1. Spread protein across the day. Aim for roughly 25 to 40 g per meal across 3 to 4 meals rather than loading dinner. [Moderate]
  2. Include high-quality protein. Eggs, fish, poultry, dairy, beef, and legumes provide essential amino acids. Animal proteins are especially efficient for building and maintaining muscle. [Strong]
  3. Use Greek yogurt and cottage cheese. They are convenient, high-protein, calcium-rich options that reduce reliance on protein powders.
  4. Try wild game in moderation. Elk, venison, and bison are lean and rich in protein, iron, zinc, and B12. If the animal was harvested with lead ammunition, lead fragments can contaminate the meat. Ask about non-lead ammunition, trim generously around wound channels, and cook to safe internal temperatures.
  5. Rotate seafood. Sardines give omega-3s and calcium, oysters give zinc, and salmon gives EPA and DHA. Favor lower-mercury choices (sardines, salmon, trout, herring, mussels, oysters) and limit high-mercury fish such as swordfish, king mackerel, and bigeye tuna. Pregnant people and young children should follow official fish-consumption guidance.
  6. Consider creatine monohydrate. It has strong evidence for improving strength and resistance-training performance. A common dose is 3 to 5 g per day. People with kidney disease should check with a doctor first. [Strong]
7. Meal Timing and Everyday Habits (4 tips)
  1. Keep most eating within daylight hours. Circadian rhythms affect glucose regulation. Avoid making late-night eating a habit. [Moderate]
  2. Finish dinner 2 to 3 hours before bed when practical. This may support sleep quality and glucose regulation. [Limited to Moderate]
  3. Drink green tea between meals. It contains catechins such as EGCG. Drinking it away from meals lessens interference with non-heme iron absorption. It contains caffeine, and evidence for strong metabolic effects is modest. [Limited]
  4. Stay hydrated. Increase fluids when sweating heavily.
8. What to Limit (7 tips)

Most of this guide is about eating more of good things. These limits often matter more.

  1. Added sugar and sugary drinks. [Strong]
  2. Excess sodium, most of which comes from packaged and restaurant food. Cooking at home gives you control. [Strong]
  3. Alcohol. Risk rises with intake, and no amount is clearly beneficial. [Strong]
  4. Processed and cured meats such as bacon, sausage, and deli meats. [Strong]
  5. Repeatedly reheated cooking oils at high temperatures, which accelerates oxidation and degradation.
  6. Aluminum foil touching food — use parchment paper instead for lining and covering. Foil leaches small amounts of aluminum into food, more with acidic or salty foods and high heat; parchment avoids it. Parchment scorches above about 425°F, so keep foil for high-heat wrapping and grilling. [Moderate]
  7. Cook in cast iron, carbon steel, or stainless steel instead of non-stick (PTFE) pans. PTFE is safe at normal cooking temperatures, but it can release fumes when overheated above about 500°F (260°C), and the coating degrades with use — cast iron has no coating to degrade. [Moderate]
9. Nutrient-Absorption Tricks (5 tips)
  1. Pair vitamin C with plant-based iron. Lemon, kiwi, oranges, and bell peppers improve absorption of non-heme iron from lentils, beans, and vegetables. [Moderate to Strong]
  2. Combine turmeric with black pepper. Piperine can substantially raise curcumin levels in the body. This is an absorption effect, and increased absorption doesn’t automatically mean a health benefit. [Limited]
  3. Grind flaxseed. Whole seeds can pass through undigested. Ground flax provides more accessible ALA omega-3, fiber, and lignans. [Moderate]
  4. Get vitamin C with collagen. Vitamin C is required for normal collagen synthesis. A normal diet usually provides enough, so mega-doses aren’t needed. [Limited]
  5. Get magnesium from food. Pumpkin seeds, almonds, spinach, legumes, and whole grains are excellent sources. [Moderate]
10. Food Safety and Storage (5 tips)
  1. Cool and refrigerate cooked rice promptly. Cooked rice left at room temperature can grow Bacillus cereus, which produces toxins that reheating doesn’t destroy. Refrigerate within about an hour and reheat until steaming hot. Don’t leave rice out to “develop resistant starch.” This is the most important safety tip in this guide.
  2. Refrigerate nuts and ground seeds. Their unsaturated fats oxidize, especially after grinding.
  3. Store olive oil in a dark, tightly sealed bottle, away from heat, light, and air.
  4. Handle cooked and cooled starches safely. The same cooling-and-refrigeration rule applies to cooked potatoes and legumes.
  5. Use wood, parchment, or glass instead of plastic where food touches it. Plastic sheds microplastics into food, especially when heated or scratched — a wooden board, a parchment cover, or a glass container sheds none. The health effects of ingested microplastics are not yet established. [Limited]
11. Cautions and Special Situations (6 notes)
  • Warfarin or other blood thinners: Keep vitamin K intake (leafy greens, broccoli) consistent rather than suddenly changing it, and talk to your prescriber.
  • Thyroid conditions: Very large amounts of raw cruciferous vegetables, sprouts, or concentrated supplements may affect thyroid function in susceptible people. Normal food portions are generally fine.
  • Kidney disease or kidney stones: Discuss protein, creatine, oxalate-rich foods (spinach, beets, nuts), and potassium with a clinician.
  • Pregnancy: Follow guidance on fish mercury, unpasteurized foods, and food safety.
  • Iron overload or low iron: Iron-absorption strategies matter differently depending on your situation.
  • Supplements: Whole foods first. Check interactions with medications.
Everyday Nutrition Foundation (8 foods)

Build your diet around:

  1. Cruciferous vegetables: broccoli, broccoli sprouts, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, cabbage.
  2. Polyphenol-rich fruits: blueberries, blackberries, raspberries, strawberries, cherries.
  3. Legumes: black lentils, red lentils, chickpeas, black beans.
  4. Healthy fats: extra virgin olive oil, walnuts, avocado, seeds.
  5. Seafood: salmon, sardines, oysters, mussels, trout.
  6. Quality protein: eggs, poultry, fish, wild game, Greek yogurt, beef in moderation.
  7. Fermented foods: kefir, plain yogurt, kimchi, sauerkraut.
  8. Herbs and spices: garlic, ginger, turmeric, rosemary, oregano, cinnamon.
Resources (5 sources)
  1. Eating on the Wild Side by Jo Robinson: produce selection, storage, and preparation.
  2. Rhonda Patrick / FoundMyFitness: sulforaphane, micronutrients, and omega-3s.
  3. Peter Attia: protein, metabolic health, and longevity nutrition.
  4. Andrew Huberman: meal timing and circadian rhythms.
  5. For a mainstream baseline, check Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health’s Nutrition Source and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans.

Guiding principle: Don’t just eat healthy foods. Choose good varieties, store them well, prepare them to preserve nutrients, and combine them intelligently. Prioritize variety over perfection. No single vegetable, supplement, or technique replaces a diverse, minimally processed, fiber-rich diet. Evidence varies by tip. Favor well-established dietary patterns over individual superfood claims, and check with a healthcare professional about your own situation.

★ Standout marks a nutrition standout — the recipe satisfies more of the 48 evidence-informed nutrition tips that apply to recipes (of 68 total) than most recipes on this page.
Yield: 4 servings | Health Focus: Gut Microbiome & Anti-Inflammatory Fats

Why It's Healthy:

  • Red miso — fermented soy paste. The fermentation breaks the beans down so they're easier to digest and builds the deep savory flavor, so a little seasons a lot. Hard boiling kills its live cultures, so miso does best stirred in at the end or, as here, as a coating rather than boiled in a soup.
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Brussels sprouts — chopping and chewing them forms sulforaphane, a compound that switches on your cells' own protective clean-up systems. Roasting until just tender keeps more of it than boiling, which washes it away.
  • Roasting, not boiling — vitamin C dissolves in water and fades in heat; roasting keeps more of it in the sprouts. Vitamin C helps you absorb iron from plant foods and builds collagen for skin and joints.
  • A little fat with the sprouts — your body can only absorb their vitamins A and K and their protective pigments dissolved in fat; without it, much passes through.
  • Pasture-raised chicken — birds that forage pick up a little more omega-3 fat, the kind that supports heart and brain, than grain-only ones. A modest edge, not a different food.
  • Organic — grown with fewer pesticide residues. The nutrition is about the same; this is about what isn't on it, not extra vitamins.

💡 Suggestion: Halve the sprouts 30–40 minutes ahead of cooking — chopping crucifers early lets the protective compounds form before heat stops them. Chop and rest.

💡 Cooking tip: For the cooked sprouts, ½–1 tsp of mustard powder restores the enzyme that cooking destroys — an easy add if you like. Mustard powder.

Ingredients
  • ⅓ cup red miso & ⅓ cup maple syrup
  • ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive-oil & 1 tsp ground cumin
  • 12 oz Brussels sprouts (trimmed and halved)
  • 3 to 4 chicken breasts (~2 lbs, cubed into 1 ½-inch pieces)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat oven to 425°F. Line a baking sheet with aluminum foil.
  2. Step 2: Whisk red miso, maple syrup, olive oil, and cumin in a bowl. Reserve a scant ¼ cup (3 tbsp) of mixture for later. Toss chicken and sprouts in the remaining marinade.
  3. Step 3: Spread everything in a single layer on the baking sheet, scraping remaining marinade on top.
  4. Step 4: Bake 8 mins. Remove, daub reserved 3 tbsp marinade on top, and bake 4 mins more.
  5. Step 5: Switch to broil for 1–2 mins until chicken is cooked through and slightly charred. Serve warm.
Substitutions: Chicken can be swapped for steak or salmon. Brussels sprouts can be swapped for green beans or mushrooms.
Yield: 4 to 6 servings | Health Focus: Cruciferous Phytonutrients & Healthy Sesame Lipids

Why It's Healthy:

  • Cabbage, kept raw — chopping cabbage lets it form the same protective compound as broccoli, which switches on your cells' clean-up systems. Eating it raw keeps that and its vitamin C, both of which heat and boiling water cut down.
  • Garlic, raw — raw garlic keeps all of its allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. Crush it and give it a few minutes before eating — that's when the allicin forms.
  • Sesame oil and seeds — sesame's own protective compounds (lignans) in plain terms: they help protect cells from everyday wear, and the seeds add a little calcium and magnesium.
  • The sesame oil does a job — fat is how your body absorbs the cabbage's fat-soluble vitamins at all.
  • Farmers market — vitamin C and folate fade a little every day after picking, so produce picked that morning starts with more of both. Folate is what your body uses to build red blood cells, and vitamin C helps absorb iron and build collagen.

💡 Cooking tip: The sesame oil isn’t just flavor — fat helps your body absorb the cabbage’s fat-soluble vitamins. Pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients.

Ingredients
  • 1 lb Taiwanese flathead cabbage or Napa cabbage
  • Kosher salt (Diamond Crystal) and black pepper
  • 2 medium garlic cloves (finely grated into paste)
  • 2 tbsp toasted sesame oil & 1 tbsp untoasted sesame seeds
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Trim outer leaves and remove the solid core from the cabbage.
  2. Step 2: Cut leaves into rough 1 ¼-inch squares; slice thick core-adjacent pieces into thin ¼-inch strips.
  3. Step 3: Wash, drain, and place cabbage in a large bowl. Sprinkle with 3 tbsp salt, scrunch with hands until mixed and beginning to soften, then let sit for 10 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Whisk garlic paste, sesame oil, ⅛ tsp salt, and ¼ tsp pepper in a small bowl.
  5. Step 5: Rinse salt off cabbage thoroughly under running water, drain well, and set aside.
  6. Step 6: Toss cabbage with dressing and sprinkle with sesame seeds right before serving. Best eaten fresh!
Tip: Taiwanese flathead cabbage offers looser, softer leaves, but Napa cabbage is an ideal substitute.
Yield: 4 servings | Health Focus: High Protein Satiety & Piperine Bioavailability

Why It's Healthy:

  • Chicken thighs — complete protein for keeping muscle; dark meat also brings a little more iron and zinc than breast meat.
  • Black pepper — piperine, its heat compound, briefly slows the liver enzymes that clear plant compounds, so you absorb more of the good compounds in the rest of the dish. (The famous '20×' number came from a purified extract in a large dose — a pinch nudges absorption, it doesn't multiply it.)
  • Sourdough — the slow ferment partly breaks down phytate, the grain compound that locks up iron and zinc, so you absorb more of both. It also raises blood sugar more gently than plain white bread (glycemic index roughly 54 vs 75).
  • Butter and cream — this is the richness, not the health part: mostly saturated fat, here for flavor and silkiness.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe lists plain unsalted butter — use grass-fed butter instead for higher omega-3s and CLA than conventional butter, same usage.

Ingredients
  • 1 tbsp whole black peppercorns & 2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil
  • 8 boneless, skinless chicken thighs (~2 lbs) & Salt
  • 2 tbsp unsalted butter & 2 tbsp minced shallot
  • 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth & ½ cup heavy cream
  • 3 thyme sprigs, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp chopped parsley
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Crush peppercorns coarsely in a bag with a mallet or saucepan.
  2. Step 2: Heat oil in a 12-inch cast-iron skillet over medium. Season chicken with salt, sear in two batches until golden (~5 mins per batch), and set aside. Pour off remaining oil.
  3. Step 3: Melt butter in skillet, cook shallot for 1 minute, then add broth, cream, thyme, and cracked peppercorns, scraping up pan browned bits.
  4. Step 4: Return chicken to skillet, bring to a simmer, and cook until internal temp reaches 165°F (6–8 mins).
  5. Step 5: Transfer chicken to plates. Stir lemon juice and parsley into the sauce until thickened, spoon over chicken, and serve.
Serving Option: Serve with crusty bread or egg noodles if desired.
Yield: 4 servings | Prep: 15 minutes | Cook: 20–25 minutes | Health Focus: High Protein & Anti-Inflammatory Spices

Why It's Healthy:

  • Chicken — lean, complete protein: all the building blocks for keeping muscle, without much fat, especially with the skin off.
  • Garlic — minced into the marinade and left to sit 20–30 minutes, which is exactly right: crushing garlic starts allicin forming, and the rest lets it finish before the heat can destroy it. Allicin is the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Greek yogurt — strained thick, so about twice the protein of regular yogurt, and full of live bacteria: they move into your gut, crowd out the harmful kind, and help with digestion and immune defenses — instead of a mayo-based sauce, for far less fat.
  • Pasture-raised chicken — birds that forage pick up a little more omega-3 fat, the kind that supports heart and brain, than grain-only ones. A modest edge, not a different food.

★ Standout recipe — satisfies 13 of the 48 recipe tips: protein 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day (0.55–0.73 g/lb/day), minimize ultra-processed (Top 10), cruciferous vegetables, chop and rest, onions, pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients, fermented foods, EVOO as main cooking fat, minimize ultra-processed (§5), protein 25–40 g per meal, high-quality protein, sodium ≤30% DV, vitamin C with plant iron

💡 Cooking tip: The marinade already does this right — garlic minced and rested 20–30 minutes before the heat, so allicin forms first. Chop and rest.

💡 Cooking tip: Lime juice in the sauce does more than brighten it — vitamin C helps absorb iron from plant foods in the meal. Vitamin C + plant iron.

💡 Cooking tip: The green sauce is olive-oil based — that fat helps absorb the fat-soluble vitamins from the herbs and vegetables it covers. Pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients.

Ingredients
  • 2 lb boneless, skinless chicken breasts or thighs
  • 2 tbsp extra virgin olive oil
  • Juice of 1 lime
  • 3–4 garlic cloves, minced
  • 1 tbsp ground cumin
  • 2 tsp paprika
  • 1 tsp dried oregano
  • 1 tsp salt
  • ½ tsp black pepper
Cilantro-Lime Green Sauce
  • 1 cup fresh cilantro
  • 1 jalapeño, roughly chopped
  • 1 garlic clove
  • Juice of 1 lime
  • ½ cup plain Greek yogurt
  • 1 tbsp extra virgin olive oil
  • ½ tsp salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Marinate the chicken. Mix olive oil, lime juice, garlic, cumin, paprika, oregano, salt and pepper. Coat chicken thoroughly. Marinate 20–30 minutes or longer in the refrigerator.
  2. Step 2: Make the green sauce. Blend cilantro, jalapeño, garlic, lime juice, Greek yogurt, olive oil and salt until smooth. Refrigerate.
  3. Step 3: Roast the chicken. Preheat oven to 425°F. Place chicken on a lightly oiled baking sheet. Roast approximately 18–25 minutes, depending on thickness, until the thickest part reaches 165°F.
  4. Step 4: Rest and serve. Let chicken rest 5 minutes before slicing. Generously spoon green sauce over the chicken.
Recommended Sides: Ginger-turmeric rice cooked in chicken broth; fresh cucumber and tomato salad; grilled zucchini or asparagus. The secret: Don't skimp on the green sauce! The combination of cumin-garlic chicken and cool, tangy cilantro-lime sauce makes this dish special.
Yield: 3–4 servings | Prep: 10 minutes | Cook: 40–45 minutes | Oven: 375°F

Golden, buttery leeks baked in garlic-Dijon cream with Gruyère and Parmesan.
Why It's Healthy:

  • Leeks — their inulin fiber is food for the good bacteria in your gut, which ferment it and make compounds that keep the gut lining healthy. Leeks also bring iron, which carries oxygen in your blood, and folate, for building red blood cells.
  • Garlic — minced into the warm sauce. Crushing garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system, and warm — not boiling — sauce is gentler on it; letting the minced garlic sit about 10 minutes before it goes in lets the allicin form first.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Cooked in the sauce, not drained away — the vitamins that dissolve in water stay in the dish instead of going down the drain.
  • Cream and Gruyère — the rich part of the dish: real flavor and calcium, and real saturated fat with it.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe adds the minced garlic straight into the warm cream — rest it about 10 minutes first and allicin forms before the heat. Chop and rest.

💡 Cooking tip: The butter and cream here do real work — fat helps absorb the leeks’ carotenoids and fat-soluble vitamins. Pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe lists plain butter — use grass-fed butter instead for higher omega-3s and CLA than conventional butter, same usage.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe lists plain heavy cream — use grass-fed cream instead for higher omega-3s and CLA than conventional cream, same usage.

Ingredients
  • 4 large leeks
  • 1 cup heavy whipping cream
  • 2 tbsp butter
  • 1 garlic clove, finely minced
  • 1 tsp Dijon mustard
  • ½ tsp salt, or to taste
  • ¼ tsp black pepper
  • ½ tsp fresh thyme (or ¼ tsp dried)
  • ¾ cup shredded Gruyère cheese
  • 2 tbsp grated Parmesan cheese
  • Small squeeze of fresh lemon juice
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Prepare the leeks. Cut off roots and dark green tops. Slice the white and light green portions crosswise into ½-inch rounds. Separate the layers and rinse thoroughly to remove dirt. Drain and arrange in a buttered glass baking dish.
  2. Step 2: Make the cream sauce. In a small saucepan, gently warm the heavy cream, butter, garlic, Dijon mustard, salt, pepper and thyme. Stir until combined. Do not boil.
  3. Step 3: Assemble. Pour the cream mixture evenly over the leeks. They should be mostly coated.
  4. Step 4: First bake. Cover the baking dish tightly with foil. Bake at 375°F for 25 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Add cheese. Remove the foil. Sprinkle Gruyère and Parmesan evenly over the top.
  6. Step 6: Finish baking. Bake uncovered for another 15–20 minutes, until the leeks are completely tender and the cheese is golden and bubbling. If needed, bake another 5–10 minutes.
  7. Step 7: Rest and serve. Let rest for 5–10 minutes. Finish with a small squeeze of fresh lemon juice and freshly cracked black pepper.
Serving Notes: Excellent alongside roasted chicken, steak, pork or fish. The leeks become sweet and tender, while the cream, garlic, Dijon and Gruyère create a rich French-style sauce. The secret: Cut the leeks into uniform ½-inch rounds, cover during the initial bake to soften them, then uncover with cheese to create that beautiful golden top.
Yield: 2–3 servings | Prep: 10 minutes

Lemon, Parmesan & Toasted Pine Nuts.
Why It's Healthy:

  • Arugula — a peppery green with a little plant iron. Plant iron is harder for your body to absorb than meat iron — which is what the lemon is for.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Olive oil on the greens — the fat is what lets your body absorb the greens' vitamins A and K and their protective pigments at all; a dressed salad feeds you more than a dry one.
  • Garlic, raw — raw garlic keeps all of its allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. Crush it and give it a few minutes before eating — that's when the allicin forms.
  • Farmers market — vitamin C and folate fade a little every day after picking, so produce picked that morning starts with more of both — and spinach can lose about half its folate in 8 days in the fridge, so fresh-picked starts ahead. Folate is what your body uses to build red blood cells, and vitamin C helps absorb iron and build collagen.
  • Organic — grown with fewer pesticide residues. The nutrition is about the same; this is about what isn't on it, not extra vitamins.

💡 Cooking tip: The olive oil in the dressing helps absorb the arugula’s carotenoids — fat with leafy greens is a feature, not just flavor. Pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients.

💡 Cooking tip: Lemon juice with the arugula isn’t just brightness — vitamin C helps absorb the iron in the greens. Vitamin C + plant iron.

Ingredients
  • 4–5 packed cups fresh baby arugula (about 4 oz)
  • ¼ cup shaved Parmigiano-Reggiano
  • 1–2 tbsp pine nuts, lightly toasted
  • Freshly cracked black pepper
  • Flaky sea salt
Fresh Lemon-Garlic Dressing
  • 2½ tbsp good-quality extra-virgin olive oil
  • 1 tbsp freshly squeezed lemon juice
  • ¼ small garlic clove, freshly pressed
  • ½ tsp finely grated fresh lemon zest
  • Freshly cracked black pepper
  • Small pinch of sea salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Toast the pine nuts. Place in a dry skillet over medium-low heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring frequently until lightly golden and fragrant. Cool.
  2. Step 2: Make the dressing. Whisk together olive oil, lemon juice, pressed garlic, lemon zest, salt, and pepper. Let sit for 3–5 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Prepare the greens. Make sure arugula is thoroughly washed and dried. Place in a large salad bowl.
  4. Step 4: Dress the salad. Drizzle dressing over the arugula a little at a time. Toss gently until lightly coated.
  5. Step 5: Finish. Add shaved Parmesan and toasted pine nuts. Finish with freshly cracked black pepper and flaky sea salt. Serve immediately.
Chef's Notes: Use a vegetable peeler for beautiful, wide Parmesan shavings. Start with less dressing; arugula should be lightly coated, never soggy. Use just a little garlic so it doesn't overpower the lemon and Parmesan. Good extra-virgin olive oil makes a noticeable difference. A few drops of aged balsamic are optional, but lemon should remain the dominant flavor.

Yield: 6–8 servings | Prep: 20 minutes | Cook: Approximately 40 minutes, plus pressure release

Whole Chicken • Fresh Ginger • Turmeric • Lemon & Herbs. A wholesome, comforting, pressure-cooker chicken soup made with simple, high-quality whole-food ingredients.
Why It's Healthy:

  • Pasture-raised chicken — birds that forage pick up a little more omega-3 fat, the kind that supports heart and brain, than grain-only ones. A modest edge, not a different food.
  • Turmeric and black pepper — turmeric's curcumin, which helps calm everyday inflammation, is poorly absorbed on its own; pepper's piperine helps you keep more of it. The dramatic study number came from a purified extract — expect a nudge, not a multiplier.
  • Carrots cooked in the broth — cooking breaks the carrots' walls so you absorb several times more of their beta-carotene (which becomes vitamin A for eyes and immunity), and because you drink the broth, nothing that leaches out is lost.
  • Lemon, added off the heat — vitamin C breaks down as it cooks, so adding it at the end keeps it working: absorbing iron, building collagen, backing up your immune system.
  • Garlic — a long simmer takes out most of its allicin, so here it's mostly the deep, mellow flavor; a little fresh crushed garlic stirred in at the end is where the health side lives.

★ Standout recipe — satisfies 17 of the 48 recipe tips: protein 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day (0.55–0.73 g/lb/day), minimize ultra-processed (Top 10), colorful produce, onions, cook tomatoes and carrots, pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients, use cooking liquids, variety of fibers, minimize ultra-processed (§5), protein 25–40 g per meal, high-quality protein, no added sugar, sodium ≤30% DV, no processed or cured meat, vitamin C with plant iron, turmeric with black pepper, rice safety

💡 Food safety: Cool and refrigerate leftover soup promptly — cooked rice left at room temperature can grow Bacillus cereus, whose toxin reheating doesn’t destroy. Rice safety.

💡 Cooking tip: Turmeric meets black pepper in this soup for a reason — piperine substantially raises curcumin absorption. Turmeric + black pepper.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe adds the smashed garlic straight into the pot — rest it about 10 minutes first and allicin forms before the heat. Chop and rest.

Chicken & Broth
  • 1 whole air-chilled, pasture-raised chicken (4–5 lb)
  • 8 cups low-sodium chicken broth
  • Kosher salt (approximately 1 tsp per 2 lb chicken for advance seasoning)
Vegetables & Aromatics
  • 1 large yellow onion, quartered
  • 3 carrots, sliced
  • 3 celery stalks, sliced
  • 5 garlic cloves, smashed
  • 1 tbsp freshly grated ginger
Seasonings
  • 2 bay leaves
  • 5–6 sprigs fresh thyme
  • 1 tsp whole black peppercorns
  • ½ tsp turmeric
Rice & Fresh Finish
  • ¾ cup jasmine or long-grain white rice, rinsed
  • ¼ cup fresh parsley, chopped
  • Juice of ½–1 fresh lemon
  • Freshly grated lemon zest (¼–½ tsp per bowl)
  • Fresh green onion, thinly sliced (about 1 tbsp per bowl)
  • Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Season the chicken. If time allows, season the chicken with approximately 1 tsp kosher salt per 2 lb. Refrigerate uncovered for several hours or overnight. Otherwise, season just before cooking.
  2. Step 2: Pressure-cook the chicken. Add chicken, onion, carrots, celery, garlic, ginger, bay leaves, thyme, peppercorns, turmeric, and chicken broth to the pressure cooker. Do not add rice, parsley, or lemon yet. Cook on High Pressure for 20 minutes. Allow a 15-minute natural release, then carefully vent the remaining pressure. Important: Check your pressure cooker's minimum liquid and maximum fill requirements. Reduce the broth if necessary to stay below the safe fill line.
  3. Step 3: Shred the chicken. Remove the chicken carefully. Discard skin and bones. Shred the breast, legs, and thighs, and pick any usable meat from the neck if desired. Return the shredded chicken to the broth. Taste and adjust salt.
  4. Step 4: Cook the rice. Stir in the rinsed rice. Cook on High Pressure for 4 minutes, followed by a 10-minute natural release. Carefully vent any remaining pressure.
  5. Step 5: Finish the soup. Stir in fresh chopped parsley and lemon juice. Taste and adjust salt, pepper, and lemon to your liking.
  6. Step 6: Garnish each bowl. Finish each serving with: freshly grated lemon zest; thinly sliced green onion; freshly ground black pepper; a little extra parsley, if desired. Add the fresh garnishes immediately before serving.
My Favorite Cooking Notes: Use a whole chicken for richer broth and a variety of tender meat. Yellow onion is the best choice for classic chicken soup flavor. Skip searing for a clean, bright broth. Keep lemon zest, lemon juice, parsley, and green onion fresh until serving. Rice absorbs broth as it sits. Add a splash of hot broth or water when reheating. Refrigerate leftovers promptly and enjoy within 3–4 days, or freeze for longer storage. The signature finish: Fresh lemon juice + lemon zest + green onion + parsley + black pepper. Simple, nourishing, flavorful, and made entirely with real ingredients.

Yield: 2–3 servings | Prep/Cook: 25 minutes

Traditional Roman Pasta | 25 Minutes | Serves 2–3. A timeless Roman pasta with silky egg-yolk sauce, sharp Pecorino Romano, crispy guanciale, and freshly cracked black pepper. No cream or butter.
Why It's Healthy:

  • Pasture-raised eggs — hens that forage pick up a little more omega-3 fat, the kind that supports heart and brain, than grain-only ones, plus more vitamin D, which is what lets your body use calcium for bones. A modest edge, not a different food.
  • Pasta — its dense structure digests slowly, so blood sugar rises more gently than with bread (glycemic index in the high 40s). Cooking it al dente keeps that structure intact.
  • Al dente limit — cooking-time studies found only a few GI points' difference; portion matters more
  • And honestly: carbonara is a rich dish — the eggs and pasta are the substance; enjoy it as one.
  • Black pepper — piperine, its heat compound, briefly slows the liver enzymes that clear plant compounds, so you absorb more of the good compounds in the rest of the dish.

💡 Cooking tip: The reserved pasta water goes into the sauce — its starch emulsifies the eggs, and the nutrients that leached into the water stay in the dish. Use cooking liquids.

Ingredients
  • 8 oz (225 g) bucatini
  • 4 oz (115 g) guanciale, diced (or pancetta)
  • 4 large egg yolks
  • 1 whole egg
  • ¾ cup finely grated Pecorino Romano
  • 1 tsp freshly cracked black pepper, plus more to taste
  • Salt, for pasta water
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Prepare the egg and cheese sauce. In a mixing bowl, whisk together the egg yolks, whole egg, grated Pecorino Romano, and black pepper until thick and creamy. Set aside.
  2. Step 2: Cook the guanciale. Place diced guanciale in a cold skillet. Turn heat to medium-low and slowly render the fat until the pieces are golden and crispy, approximately 6–10 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave the rendered fat in the pan.
  3. Step 3: Cook the pasta. Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Salt lightly. Cook bucatini until al dente. Reserve at least 1 cup of pasta water before draining.
  4. Step 4: Make the carbonara. Transfer the hot bucatini directly into the skillet with the guanciale and rendered fat. Toss thoroughly. Remove the skillet from the heat and allow it to cool for 30–45 seconds. Add the egg and cheese mixture, tossing continuously. Gradually add reserved pasta water, one tablespoon at a time, until the sauce becomes silky, glossy, and coats every strand. Important: Never add the egg mixture over direct heat. Residual heat cooks the eggs without scrambling them.
  5. Step 5: Serve. Twirl pasta into warm bowls. Distribute the crispy guanciale throughout. Finish with freshly grated Pecorino Romano and another generous crack of black pepper.
Secrets to Excellent Carbonara: Use guanciale: Traditional Italian cured pork with incredible flavor. Pancetta is the next-best substitute. Grate cheese finely: This helps it incorporate smoothly. Save pasta water: Its starch helps emulsify the eggs

NYT-Inspired Pressure Cooker Version (Yedi).
Why It's Healthy:

  • Navy beans — fiber that feeds your gut bacteria and slows digestion so blood sugar rises gently, plus plant protein, iron for carrying oxygen in your blood, folate for building red blood cells, and potassium for blood pressure.
  • Beans plus vitamin C — beans' iron is the plant kind, which your body absorbs far better with vitamin C in the same meal (that's the baked-potato pairing). Vitamin C also builds collagen for skin and joints.
  • Pressure cooking — the intense heat cuts the beans' phytic acid by about a third. Phytic acid locks up iron and zinc, so less of it means more of both reaches you.
  • Carrots cooked in the broth — cooking breaks the carrots' walls so you absorb several times more of their beta-carotene (which becomes vitamin A for eyes and immunity), and because you drink the broth, nothing that leaches out is lost.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.

Keep the 20-minute natural release, and check the ham hocks are fall-apart tender before serving, since they cook in the same time. Soak and cook beans.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe lists plain butter — use grass-fed butter instead for higher omega-3s and CLA than conventional butter, same usage.

Yield: Approximately 1½ quarts | Style: Classic French-style egg custard | Chilling: 6 hours minimum, preferably overnight | Churning: Approximately 20–30 minutes

Waring 166P Ice Cream Parlor. Classic French-style egg custard.
Why It's Healthy:

  • A treat — the teaching here is ingredient quality, not a health food.
  • Frozen fruit — fruit frozen right at ripe keeps its vitamin C, beta-carotene and folate as well as fresh does; those fade in fresh fruit sitting in transit instead.
  • Pasture-raised eggs — hens that forage pick up a little more omega-3 fat, the kind that supports heart and brain, than grain-only ones, plus more vitamin D, which is what lets your body use calcium for bones. A modest edge, not a different food.
  • Milk and cream — the base is rich: that's what ice cream is. Real ingredients, eaten as the treat it is.
  • Lemon juice — a little vitamin C, and brightness that makes the fruit taste more like itself; the vanilla is flavor without sugar.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe lists plain whole milk and heavy cream — use grass-fed milk and cream instead for higher omega-3s and CLA than conventional dairy, same usage.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe gives you a choice of parchment paper or plastic wrap — choose the parchment. It presses against the ice cream just as well, with no plastic touching the food. Wood, parchment, or glass instead of plastic.

Choose ONE Fruit
  • Peach: 1¼ lb ripe fresh peaches, peeled and pitted.
  • Strawberry: 1¼ lb ripe fresh strawberries, washed and hulled.
Fruit Preparation
  • ¼ cup granulated sugar
  • 1 tbsp fresh lemon juice
  • 1 tbsp mild honey
Creamy Custard Base
  • 2 cups whole milk
  • 1½ cups heavy cream
  • 6 large egg yolks
  • ¼ cup granulated sugar
  • ¼ tsp kosher salt
  • 1 tsp pure vanilla extract
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Prepare the Fruit. Peel and pit 1¼ lb peaches OR wash and hull 1¼ lb strawberries. Slice all the fruit. Combine in a saucepan with: ¼ cup granulated sugar; 1 tbsp fresh lemon juice; 1 tbsp mild honey. Let macerate for 20 minutes. Important: Do not reserve any fruit pieces. All the fruit will be puréed completely smooth. We want absolutely no chunks in the finished ice cream.
  2. Step 2: Cook and Concentrate the Fruit. Cook the fruit mixture over medium-low heat for approximately 15–20 minutes, stirring frequently. Cook until the fruit is very soft and the mixture is thick, syrupy and noticeably reduced. Allow excess water to evaporate. This is especially important with strawberries, which contain considerable water. Do not aggressively boil or caramelize. Let cool for 10 minutes. Transfer the entire mixture, including its syrup, to a blender. Blend until completely smooth. Pass through a fine-mesh strainer to remove strawberry seeds, peach fibers and any remaining solids. Refrigerate.
  3. Step 3: Make the Custard. Combine in a saucepan: 2 cups whole milk; 1½ cups heavy cream; ¼ cup granulated sugar; ¼ tsp kosher salt. Heat over medium heat until steaming. Do not boil. In a separate bowl, whisk 6 large egg yolks. Slowly whisk 1 cup of the hot dairy mixture into the egg yolks. Pour the tempered egg mixture back into the saucepan with the remaining 2½ cups dairy. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until the custard reaches approximately 175°F and coats the back of a spoon. Do not boil.
  4. Step 4: Strain and Combine. Pour the custard through a fine-mesh strainer into a clean bowl. Add: All of the cooked, puréed and strained fruit mixture; 1 tsp pure vanilla extract. Whisk thoroughly until completely uniform. The finished base should be entirely smooth, with no fruit chunks, seeds or fibers.
  5. Step 5: Chill Thoroughly. Place the bowl over an ice bath and stir until completely cool. Cover and refrigerate for at least 6 hours, preferably overnight. The mixture must be thoroughly cold before churning. This helps the Waring freeze the mixture faster, producing smaller ice crystals.
  6. Step 6: Churn in the Waring 166P. Pour the thoroughly chilled mixture into the freezing canister. Do not exceed the maximum fill level. Install the dasher and lid. Prepare the ice-and-salt freezing bath according to the Waring 166P instructions. Churn approximately 20–30 minutes, or until thick and creamy, similar to firm soft serve. Do not rely exclusively on the clock. Watch the consistency.
  7. Step 7: Harden. Immediately transfer the finished ice cream to a shallow, airtight freezer container. Smooth the surface. Press parchment paper or plastic wrap directly against the ice cream. Seal and freeze for at least 4 hours, preferably overnight. Keep the container toward the back of the freezer, where the temperature is most stable. Let stand for approximately 5–10 minutes before scooping.
Yield: 8–10 summer rolls | Prep: 30 minutes | Total time: 40–45 minutes

Fresh shrimp, garden cucumber, herbs, rice noodles & homemade peanut dipping sauce.
Why It's Healthy:

  • Raw vegetables — vitamin C fades with heat and time, so vegetables rolled up raw keep all of theirs: immune support, collagen for skin, and help absorbing iron.
  • Shrimp — lean protein for very few calories, plus selenium, a mineral your thyroid needs to make its hormones and your cells need to defend themselves. A small serving brings about half a day's selenium.
  • Carrots with the peanut sauce — the sauce's fat is what lets you absorb the carrots' beta-carotene; raw carrots alone give you only a fraction of it.
  • Garlic, raw — raw garlic keeps all of its allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. Crush it and give it a few minutes before eating — that's when the allicin forms.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Farmers market — vitamin C and folate fade a little every day after picking, so produce picked that morning starts with more of both. Folate is what your body uses to build red blood cells, and vitamin C helps absorb iron and build collagen.
  • Organic — grown with fewer pesticide residues. The nutrition is about the same; this is about what isn't on it, not extra vitamins.

💡 Cooking tip: The peanut sauce isn’t just a dip — its fat helps absorb the carrots’ beta-carotene. Pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients.

💡 Cooking tip: Lime juice with the vegetables helps absorb non-heme iron from the plant foods in the rolls. Vitamin C + plant iron.

💡 Cooking tip: The rice vinegar in the peanut sauce isn’t just brightness — vinegar with a carb-heavy meal may modestly lower post-meal glucose. Vinegar with carb-heavy meals.

💡 Suggestion: For make-ahead rolls, skip wrapping each one in plastic wrap — store them in an airtight container lined with a damp kitchen towel instead. They stay moist and don’t stick, with no plastic touching the food. Wood, parchment, or glass instead of plastic.

Summer Rolls
  • 1 lb medium or large shrimp, peeled and deveined
  • 8–10 rice paper wrappers (8–9 inch)
  • 3–4 oz dry rice vermicelli noodles
  • 1–2 cucumbers, cut into thin matchsticks
  • 2 carrots, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks
  • 1 head butter lettuce or green leaf lettuce
  • ½ cup fresh basil leaves
  • ½ cup fresh mint leaves
  • ½ cup fresh cilantro leaves
  • 3 scallions, thinly sliced
  • 1 tbsp olive or avocado oil
  • Salt and black pepper
Homemade Peanut Dipping Sauce
  • ⅓ cup creamy peanut butter, preferably unsweetened
  • ¼ cup hoisin sauce
  • ½ cup warm water
  • 1 tbsp fresh lime juice
  • 1 tsp rice vinegar
  • 1 garlic clove, finely grated
  • 1–2 tsp Sriracha, optional
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Prepare the Peanut Sauce.
    1. Combine ⅓ cup peanut butter, ¼ cup hoisin, 1 tbsp lime juice, 1 tsp rice vinegar, 1 grated garlic clove and 1–2 tsp Sriracha.
    2. Gradually whisk in ½ cup warm water until smooth.
    3. Adjust consistency with additional water if needed.
    4. Refrigerate until ready to serve.
  2. Step 2: Cook the Shrimp.
    1. Pat 1 lb shrimp dry.
    2. Season lightly with salt and black pepper.
    3. Heat 1 tbsp olive or avocado oil in a skillet over medium-high heat.
    4. Cook shrimp approximately 1–2 minutes per side, until opaque and cooked through (145°F internal temperature).
    5. Allow to cool.
    6. Slice shrimp in half lengthwise.
  3. Step 3: Prepare the Noodles.
    1. Cook 3–4 oz rice vermicelli according to package instructions.
    2. Drain and rinse thoroughly under cold water.
    3. Drain very well and set aside.
  4. Step 4: Prepare the Vegetables & Herbs.
    1. Cut cucumbers and 2 carrots into thin matchsticks.
    2. Thinly slice 3 scallions.
    3. Wash and thoroughly dry lettuce, basil, mint and cilantro.
    4. Separate lettuce leaves into manageable pieces.
  5. Step 5: Assemble the Rolls.
    1. Fill a large shallow dish with room-temperature water.
    2. Dip one rice paper wrapper into the water for approximately 5–10 seconds. Remove while still slightly firm; it will continue softening.
    3. Lay wrapper flat on a clean, damp cutting board.
    4. Place a piece of lettuce near the bottom third.
    5. Add a small handful of rice noodles.
    6. Add cucumber, carrot and scallions.
    7. Add generous amounts of basil, mint and cilantro.
    8. Place 3–4 shrimp halves across the filling.
  6. Step 6: Roll.
    1. Fold the bottom edge over the filling.
    2. Fold both sides inward.
    3. Roll forward tightly, like a burrito.
    4. Place seam-side down.
    5. Repeat with remaining ingredients.
Serving: Serve immediately with homemade peanut dipping sauce and fresh lime wedges. For best results, serve fresh. If making ahead, wrap each roll individually in plastic wrap and refrigerate for up to one day. Avoid stacking.
Variations:
  1. Classic Shrimp & Pork — Add thinly sliced cooked pork tenderloin alongside the shrimp. A traditional Vietnamese combination.
  2. Avocado Summer Rolls — Add thin slices of avocado for extra creaminess and healthy fats.
  3. Spicy Summer Rolls — Add thinly sliced jalapeño and extra Sriracha to the peanut sauce.
  4. Chicken Summer Rolls — Substitute grilled or poached chicken breast for shrimp.
  5. Extra Vegetable Rolls — Add bean sprouts, shredded cabbage, daikon radish or bell pepper.
My Favorite Combination: Shrimp + garden cucumber + carrot + rice noodles + butter lettuce + lots of fresh basil, mint and cilantro + homemade peanut sauce. Cooking tip: Don't overstuff the rolls, don't oversoak the rice paper, and dry the vegetables and noodles thoroughly. These three things make the biggest difference in getting beautiful, tightly rolled summer rolls.
Oven: 350°F | First bake: 80 minutes | Cool: 20–30 minutes | Second bake: 20 minutes

A simple, classic baked potato with extra-crispy, salty skin and a light, fluffy interior.
Why It's Healthy:

  • Let it cool 20–30 minutes — as cooked potato cools, some of its starch re-forms into resistant starch: starch your own enzymes can't break down, so it reaches your gut bacteria, which feed on it and make compounds that keep the gut lining healthy.
  • Chilled potatoes — a cold potato has roughly 40% more resistant starch than a hot one, and gentle reheating keeps most of it. A long fridge chill builds more.
  • Honest limit — 2019 trial found no significant 3-hour blood-sugar difference; gut benefit is the solid part
  • The skin — much of the potato's fiber lives in and right under the skin. Fiber feeds gut bacteria and slows digestion, so skin-on is the more filling, steadier choice.
  • The potato's own vitamin C helps you absorb its iron — a small built-in pairing.
  • Butter, cheddar and sour cream — the indulgent layer. Real ingredients, and the potato underneath is the point.

💡 Cooking tip: This recipe already builds in the cool — letting the potato rest 20–30 minutes between bakes creates resistant starch that feeds gut bacteria, and reheating keeps most of it. Cook, cool, reheat potatoes.

💡 Cooking tip: The potato’s own vitamin C helps absorb its iron. Vitamin C + plant iron.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe lists plain butter among the toppings — use grass-fed butter instead for higher omega-3s and CLA than conventional butter, same usage.

Ingredients
  • 1 large russet potato
  • Extra virgin olive oil
  • Kosher salt
  • Freshly ground black pepper
  • Butter
  • Sharp cheddar cheese, freshly grated
  • Sour cream
  • Fresh green onion or garlic chives, finely chopped
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Prepare the potato. Preheat oven to 350°F. Scrub the russet potato thoroughly and dry completely. Pierce 4–6 times with a fork.
  2. Step 2: Season the skin. Rub the entire potato generously with olive oil. Coat all sides with kosher salt.
  3. Step 3: First bake. Place directly on the oven rack, with a baking sheet underneath to catch drippings. Bake at 350°F for 80 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Cool. Remove from the oven and let the potato cool for approximately 20–30 minutes. This allows steam to escape and helps develop a better texture.
  5. Step 5: Second bake. Return the potato directly to the oven rack and bake at 350°F for another 20 minutes. The skin should be nicely crisp and the inside soft and fluffy.
  6. Step 6: Open and fluff. Remove from the oven. Cut a lengthwise slit across the top and gently squeeze the ends to open. Fluff the interior with a fork.
  7. Step 7: Add toppings. While piping hot, add butter, freshly grated sharp cheddar, salt, and freshly ground black pepper. Let the cheese melt.
  8. Step 8: Finish. Top with a generous spoonful of sour cream and finely chopped fresh green onion or garlic chives.
The finishing touch: Serve immediately while the skin is crispy, the center is steaming hot, and the cheddar is melted. Don't wrap in foil at any point. The key: Olive oil, plenty of kosher salt, baking uncovered, and allowing the potato to cool between the two bakes.

★ Standout combination: Senate Bean Soup + Baked Potato covers 20 of the 48 recipe tips together — the potato adds the cook-cool-reheat resistant starch and the vitamin C that pairs with the beans’ iron. Tips covered together: fiber 30 g/day, legumes, protein 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day (0.55–0.73 g/lb/day), minimize ultra-processed (Top 10), onions, cook tomatoes and carrots, pair fat with fat-soluble nutrients, cook, cool, reheat potatoes, use cooking liquids, variety of fibers, legumes and resistant starch, vinegar with carb-heavy meals, minimize ultra-processed (§5), protein 25–40 g per meal, high-quality protein, no added sugar, sodium ≤30% DV, no processed or cured meat, vitamin C with plant iron, magnesium from food

Servings: 2–4 | Prep: 10 minutes | Cook: 20–35 minutes | Oven: 250°F

Why It's Healthy:

  • Salmon — the one dish here with real vitamin D (about a full day's worth in a serving). Vitamin D is what lets your body absorb calcium for bones, and most people run low. Plus omega-3 fats, which help keep heart rhythm steady and build brain cells.
  • Garlic, raw — raw garlic keeps all of its allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. Crush it and give it a few minutes before eating — that's when the allicin forms. Resting in the fridge lets it form fully.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Greek yogurt — strained thick, so about twice the protein of regular yogurt, and full of live bacteria: they move into your gut, crowd out the harmful kind, and help with digestion and immune defenses — far less fat than a mayo-based sauce.
  • The gentle 250°F bake — harsh high heat can damage salmon's omega-3 fats; low and slow keeps them, and the oil and lemon keep the fish moist without adding fat.

★ Standout recipe — satisfies 14 of the 48 recipe tips: fatty fish twice a week, minimize ultra-processed (Top 10), colorful produce, onions, variety of fibers, fermented foods, fatty fish — EPA and DHA omega-3s, nuts and seeds, minimize ultra-processed (§5), protein 25–40 g per meal, high-quality protein, lower-mercury seafood, sodium ≤30% DV, vitamin C with plant iron

Yield: 4 to 6 servings | Oven: 400 degrees, then 300 degrees

Why It's Healthy:

  • The potatoes cook in the cream — the vitamins that dissolve in water stay in the dish instead of being drained away.
  • Butter, half-and-half and cheese — this is an indulgent dish and doesn't pretend otherwise: the richness is the point, in a modest portion.
  • Honest gap — effectively no vitamin D here; that's why the pairing points to the salmon.
  • Serve it as the indulgent side, with something lean and green alongside.

💡 Suggestion: For leftovers, cool the gratin promptly and refrigerate — cooling creates resistant starch, and reheating keeps most of it. Cook, cool, reheat.

💡 Cooking tip: Nothing is drained from this dish, so the water-soluble vitamins that leach out stay in the cream sauce. Use cooking liquids.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe lists plain unsalted butter — use grass-fed butter instead for higher omega-3s and CLA than conventional butter, same usage.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe covers the dish with foil — use parchment paper instead. It holds in moisture the same way at 375°F, with no aluminum touching the food. Parchment instead of foil.

Ingredients
  • 3 to 4 pounds potatoes, peeled and cut into ¼-inch slices
  • Kosher salt and black pepper
  • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter
  • 2 to 3 cups half-and-half or heavy cream
  • ¼ cup grated Parmesan or Gruyère
  • Pinch of nutmeg
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat oven to 400 degrees. Seasoning each layer with salt and pepper as you go, layer the potatoes in a 10- or 12-inch ovenproof skillet.
  2. Step 2: Dot the top with 2 tablespoons butter. Pour in half-and-half. (It should come about ¾ of the way to the top.)
  3. Step 3: Bring to a boil over medium-high heat. Reduce to low and cook for 10 minutes, uncovered, until the half-and-half has reduced by about half.
  4. Step 4: Transfer to the oven and bake until the top is golden brown, about 10 minutes. Reduce heat to 300 degrees and cook until the potatoes are fork tender and the top is nicely browned, about 8 minutes more. Top with grated cheese and return to the oven until the cheese is melty and golden brown, about 3 to 5 minutes. Sprinkle with a pinch of nutmeg, if using, and serve.
Yield: 6 to 8 servings | Oven: 300 degrees, then 400 degrees

Why It's Healthy:

  • The low, slow braise — hours of gentle heat melt tough connective tissue into gelatin, which is why the meat turns silky. Gelatin brings the amino acids skin and joint tissue are made from, though it isn't a complete protein on its own.
  • Garlic — a long simmer takes out most of its allicin, so here it's mostly the deep, mellow flavor; a little fresh crushed garlic stirred in at the end is where the health side lives.
  • Pasture-raised ribs — animals that forage pick up a little more omega-3 fat, the kind that supports heart and brain, than grain-only ones. A modest edge, not a different food.
  • Balance — this is a rich cut. The baked potato it points to does real work alongside: vitamin C that helps you absorb iron, potassium for blood pressure, and fiber that feeds your gut bacteria.

💡 Suggestion: The recipe adds the smashed garlic straight into the pot — rest it about 10 minutes first and allicin forms before the heat. Chop and rest.

💡 Cooking tip: The apple cider vinegar in the braise isn’t just tang — vinegar with a carb-heavy meal may modestly lower post-meal glucose. Vinegar with carb-heavy meals.

💡 Suggestion: The glaze lists plain unsalted butter — use grass-fed butter instead for higher omega-3s and CLA than conventional butter, same usage.

For the Ribs
  • 1 tablespoon garlic powder
  • 1 tablespoon onion powder
  • 1 tablespoon smoked paprika
  • 1 teaspoon kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal)
  • ½ teaspoon black pepper
  • 3 to 4 pounds St. Louis- or country-style pork ribs, cut into individual ribs (see Tips)
  • 2 tablespoons vegetable or canola oil for searing, plus more if necessary
  • 1 medium onion, sliced
  • 4 cloves garlic, smashed
  • 1 cup pure pineapple juice
  • ⅓ cup soy sauce
  • 2 tablespoons apple cider vinegar
  • 1 tablespoon Worcestershire sauce
For the Glaze
  • ½ cup ketchup
  • ¼ cup honey
  • 2 to 3 tablespoons (light or dark) brown sugar
  • 1 tablespoon unsalted butter
For serving
  • Cooked white rice, cornbread or coleslaw, optional.
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Prepare the ribs. Heat the oven to 300 degrees. In a small bowl, stir together the garlic powder, onion powder, smoked paprika, salt and pepper. Pat the ribs dry with paper towels and rub the seasoning evenly over every side.
  2. Step 2: Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high until shimmering. Working in batches so the pot is not crowded and lowering the heat as necessary to avoid scorching, sear the ribs on all sides until deeply browned, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate as they finish.
  3. Step 3: Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion and garlic to the pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and just beginning to color, 2 to 3 minutes. Pour in the pineapple juice, soy sauce, vinegar and Worcestershire sauce, scraping up any browned bits from the bottom of the pot.
  4. Step 4: Return the ribs and any accumulated juices to the pot, nestling them into the liquid — it should come about halfway up the ribs. Cover and transfer to the oven. Bake for 1 hour, remove the ribs from the oven and gently toss and rearrange. Return to oven and cook another 45 minutes to 1 hour, until very tender but not falling off the bone. Remove the Dutch oven from the oven and uncover it. Raise the oven temperature to 400 degrees.
  5. Step 5: While the oven heats, prepare the glaze. Combine the ketchup, honey, brown sugar and butter in a small saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, reduce heat to medium-low and cook, stirring occasionally, for about 5 minutes, until the glaze is thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
  6. Step 6: Transfer the ribs to a rack set on a baking sheet. Pour or brush the glaze over the ribs, turning each piece to coat. Return the ribs to the oven and cook for 5 to 7 minutes, until caramelized. If you'd like, skim the fat from the braising liquid in the pot. Serve the ribs hot, with the braising liquid spooned over rice or reduced into a sauce on the side.
Tips: Country-style ribs or a St. Louis cut both work. Baby backs cook a touch faster — start checking at the 1 hour 30 minute mark. Ask the butcher to cut the rack into individual ribs, or do it yourself with a sharp chef's knife between the bones before seasoning.
Yield: About 24 cookies | Prep: 15 min | Cook: 15 min | Total: 30 min

These are the most requested cookies in my family — I have made them more times than I can count. Coconut is the underrated one here: paired with nutty brown butter, the two flavors are magic together. Then there is the dark chocolate — ever so slightly crisp on the edge, but soft, chewy, and gooey in the middle, and heavy on the chocolate. If you are a real chocolate lover, do half semisweet chocolate chips and half chopped chocolate chunks for bigger pockets of chocolate!
Why It's Healthy:

Adapted from a cookbook.

  • A treat — the point is ingredient quality, not a health food.
  • Dark chocolate — cocoa flavanols help blood vessels relax so blood flows more easily. Darker chocolate means more flavanols and less sugar.
  • Coconut flour — very high in fiber for a flour, and fiber feeds gut bacteria and steadies blood sugar. In a cookie the amount is small — a better ingredient, not a health food.
  • Sesame seeds — a little calcium, which bones are built from, and sesame's own protective compounds; a sprinkle's worth, so think flavor first.
  • Eggs — complete protein with every building block your muscles need to repair, plus choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical.
Ingredients
  • 1 cup (2 sticks) salted butter
  • ¾ cup packed light or dark brown sugar
  • ½ cup granulated sugar
  • 2 large eggs
  • 1 tablespoon pure vanilla extract
  • 1¼ cups all-purpose flour
  • ½ cup coconut flour
  • 1 teaspoon baking soda
  • ½ teaspoon fine pink Himalayan salt
  • 1½ cups chopped bittersweet chocolate chunks or chips
  • 2 tablespoons sesame seeds
  • flaky sea salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat the oven. Preheat the oven to 350°F. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper.
  2. Step 2: Brown the butter. Place the butter in a small skillet over medium heat. Cook until the butter begins to brown, about 5 minutes. Transfer to a large heatproof bowl and set aside to cool for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally.
  3. Step 3: Mix the dough. To the brown butter, add the brown sugar, granulated sugar, eggs, and vanilla and stir until smooth. Add the all-purpose flour, coconut flour, baking soda, and pink salt and mix until just combined. If your dough feels too dry, stir in up to 2 tablespoons of water. Gently fold in the chocolate and sesame seeds, mixing just enough to combine.
  4. Step 4: Shape the cookies. Using 1 generously rounded tablespoon for each, roll the dough into balls. Arrange the balls on the prepared baking sheets, spacing them 2 inches apart. Gently press the dough down to slightly flatten.
  5. Step 5: Bake, tap, and bake again. Bake the cookies for 8 minutes. Remove the baking sheets from the oven and tap them firmly against the counter a few times to flatten the cookies. Return to the oven and bake until the cookies are just beginning to set on the edges, 2 to 3 minutes more.
  6. Step 6: Salt and cool. Sprinkle the cookies with flaky salt and let them cool on the baking sheets; they will continue to cook slightly. Enjoy the cookies warm (highly recommended) or let cool and store at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 4 days.
Health Focus: Protein & Calcium

Adapted from Soulful Harvest.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Cheese — protein and calcium, which bones are built from, in a small, flavorful amount. It's rich and salty, so here it works as a seasoning, not the main event.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
  • It's still cheese spread — rich and salty. The homemade part means you control what goes in, not that it's light.

Adapted from Soulful Harvest.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Tomatoes — lycopene, the red pigment, helps protect the heart and blood vessels, and cooking tomatoes in a little oil makes it much easier for your body to absorb: one case where cooked beats raw.
  • Carrots and root vegetables — beta-carotene, the orange pigment your body turns into vitamin A for your eyes and immune system. Cooking them and eating them with a little fat helps you absorb far more than raw carrots alone.
  • Celery — hydration, fiber, and crunch for almost no calories.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
  • Beef and lamb — iron in the form your body absorbs best, plus vitamin B12, which you need to make red blood cells and keep nerves working; running low leaves you tired and foggy.
  • Short ribs are a fatty cut — this is a rich, occasional dish; the vegetables in the pot are doing the balancing.
Ingredients
  • 5LBS. SHORT RIBS
  • 1½ TEASPOONS SALT
  • ½ TEASPOON BLACK PEPPER
  • 6 TABLESPOONS EVOO
  • 1 ONION, CHOPPED
  • 2 CARROTS, CHOPPED
  • 3 CELERY STOCKS, CHOPPED
  • ½ CUP TOMATO PASTE
  • 2 CUPS RED WINE
  • ½ CUP RED WINE VINEGAR
  • 1 QUART BEEF STOCK
  • 2 CUPS CHICKEN STOCK
  • 2 FRESH THYME SPRIGS
  • 1 BAY LEAF
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the oven to 325 F.
  2. Step 2: Dry the ribs with towels and season them with the salt and pepper.
  3. Step 3: Heat the oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high heat and brown the ribs in batches so the pot is not crowded, turning often, about 8–10 minutes; set aside.
  4. Step 4: Lower the heat and cook the onion, carrots and celery in the oil left in the pot, stirring, until soft and lightly browned, about 8–10 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Stir in the tomato paste, wine and vinegar and boil over high heat until the liquid is reduced by half.
  6. Step 6: Add both stocks, the thyme and the bay leaf and bring to a boil.
  7. Step 7: Return the ribs and any juices from the plate to the pot.
  8. Step 8: Cover, move to the oven and braise until the meat is very tender, 2 to 2½ hours.
  9. Step 9: Take the ribs out and set aside. Strain the cooking liquid through a colander into a bowl without pressing on the solids; throw the solids away.
  10. Step 10: Rest the liquid until the fat rises, then skim the fat off the top.
  11. Step 11: Put the liquid back in the Dutch oven, bring it to a strong simmer and cook, stirring now and then, until reduced by one-third, about 18–20 minutes.
  12. Step 12: Taste and adjust with salt and pepper.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Portion is the point — pork belly is the fattiest cut there is; a small, crisp piece with sharp sides is the satisfying way to eat it.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Pork — complete protein for muscles, plus thiamine (vitamin B1), which your body needs to turn food into energy.
Ingredients
  • 9 LBS. PORK BELLY
  • 8 CUPS SALT
  • ½ CUP JUNIPER BERRIES, TOASTED AND CRUSHED
  • ½ CUP ALLSPICE, TOASTED AND CRUSHED
  • 2 CUPS BROWN SUGAR
  • 2 BIG HANDFULS OF THYME SPRIGS
  • 1 CUP GARLIC, MINCED
  • ½ CUP BLACK PEPPERCORNS, TOASTED
  • 12 PIECES CINNAMON STICKS, ALL BUSTED UP
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Stir together the salt, juniper, allspice, brown sugar, thyme sprigs, minced garlic, peppercorns and broken-up cinnamon sticks to make the cure.
  2. Step 2: Spread one-third of the cure in the bottom of a hotel pan and lay the pork bellies on top.
  3. Step 3: Cover the bellies with the rest of the cure and refrigerate 6 hours.
  4. Step 4: After 6 hours, turn the bellies over and rub the cure over all surfaces; refrigerate another 18 hours.
  5. Step 5: When curing is done, rinse the bellies and let them dry.
  6. Step 6: Roast in an oven preheated to 500 F for 50 minutes.
  7. Step 7: Drop the heat to 325 F and roast 3 hours more.
  8. Step 8: Remove from the oven and cool 1 hour.
  9. Step 9: Wrap in plastic wrap, chill and set aside for later use.

Adapted from Soulful Harvest.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A big, rich cut — built to share.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Carrots and root vegetables — beta-carotene, the orange pigment your body turns into vitamin A for your eyes and immune system. Cooking them and eating them with a little fat helps you absorb far more than raw carrots alone.
  • Celery — hydration, fiber, and crunch for almost no calories.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
Ingredients
  • 8 PORK SHANKS
  • 2 CUPS FLOUR
  • 1 CUP EVOO
  • 3 ONIONS, ROUGH CHOP
  • 8 CARROTS, ROUGH CHOP
  • 10 CELERY RIBS, ROUGH CHOP
  • A WHOLE BUNCH OF GARLIC CLOVES
  • A GOOD BOTTLE OF RED WINE
  • 2 QUARTS BEEF STOCK
  • 2 QUARTS CHICKEN STOCK
  • A HANDFUL OF ROSEMARY SPRIGS
  • 6 OR 7 LAUREL LEAVES
  • SALT AND PEPPER, TO YOUR TASTE
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the oven to 375 F.
  2. Step 2: Coat/season the shanks with the flour, salt and black pepper.
  3. Step 3: Heat the EVOO in a Dutch oven over medium heat and start searing the shanks.
  4. Step 4: Move the seared shanks to a platter and set aside.
  5. Step 5: Add the onions, carrots, celery and garlic to the Dutch oven and cook slowly 8–10 minutes.
  6. Step 6: Add the wine and reduce it by half.
  7. Step 7: Add the beef and chicken stocks, rosemary, laurel, salt and black pepper and bring to a rolling boil.
  8. Step 8: Return the shanks to the pot and lower the heat to a strong simmer.
  9. Step 9: Put the lid on and cook in the preheated oven for 3 hours.
  10. Step 10: Move the braised shanks to a platter, cover with foil, and make the Pan Reduction Sauce (below).

Adapted from Soulful Harvest.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Eggs — complete protein with every building block your muscles need to repair, plus choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical and which most people don't get enough of.
  • Leafy greens — folate for making new cells and red blood, vitamin K for clotting and bones, and natural nitrates for blood flow, all for almost no calories.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Cheese — protein and calcium, which bones are built from, in a small, flavorful amount. It's rich and salty, so here it works as a seasoning, not the main event.
  • Pork — complete protein for muscles, plus thiamine (vitamin B1), which your body needs to turn food into energy.
Ingredients
  • 1 LEMON
  • 1 TEASPOON CHOPPED FRESH SAGE
  • 1 TEASPOON CHOPPED FRESH THYME
  • 1 TEASPOON SALT PLUS 1 PINCH
  • 1 TEASPOON BLACK PEPPER
  • 2 PORK TENDERLOINS
  • ½ CUP ALL-PURPOSE FLOUR
  • 3 EGGS, BEATEN
  • 3 CUPS PANKO BREADCRUMBS
  • ¾ CUP PARMESAN CHEESE, GRATED
  • 3 TABLESPOONS CAPERS
  • 4 CUPS ARUGULA
  • 2 TABLESPOONS EVOO
  • 4 HARD-BOILED EGGS, PEELED AND COARSELY CHOPPED
Preparation
  1. Step 1: With a small sharp knife, cut all peel and white pith from the lemon; quarter it lengthwise, then slice it thinly crosswise. Cover and chill the slices; throw the peel away.
  2. Step 2: In a small bowl, stir together the sage, thyme, 1 teaspoon of the salt and 1 teaspoon ground pepper.
  3. Step 3: Slice the tenderloins crosswise into ¾-inch-thick pieces, then pound each piece between two sheets of plastic wrap with a mallet to ¼-inch thickness.
  4. Step 4: Scatter the sage mixture over both sides of each cutlet.
  5. Step 5: Set up breading bowls: flour in one bowl, the beaten eggs in another, and the breadcrumbs mixed with the cheese in a third.
  6. Step 6: One cutlet at a time: dredge in flour and shake off the excess, dip in egg to coat, then press into the breadcrumb mixture on both sides so it sticks. Chill the breaded cutlets at least 30 minutes.
  7. Step 7: Heat the oven to 250 F.
  8. Step 8: Heat oil (for the skillet; amount not listed) in a heavy skillet over medium-high heat and cook the pork until browned and cooked through, about 2 minutes per side.
  9. Step 9: Move the cutlets to a baking sheet and keep them warm in the oven.
  10. Step 10: Plate the cutlets and scatter the capers and lemon slices over them.
  11. Step 11: Toss the arugula with the 2 tablespoons EVOO and salt, pile it over the pork, and sprinkle the chopped eggs on top.

To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
