Ingredients
  • 3 QUARTS CHICKEN STOCK
  • 3 CUPS ARBORIO RICE
  • 2 ONIONS, SMALL DICE
  • ¼ CUP GARLIC, MINCED
  • 2 LBS. MUSHROOMS, SLICED
  • 2 TABLESPOONS TRUFFLE OIL
  • 1 CUP PARMESAN CHEESE
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Bring the chicken stock to a boil, then lower the heat to a strong simmer and keep it hot.
  2. Step 2: In a saucepan over medium heat, cook the onions in oil (the method refers to oil/aromatic oil; no separate oil quantity is listed) until caramelised, about 4–5 minutes. Note: the method also calls for the garlic and the sliced mushrooms in the pan aromatics, though the printed steps name the onions explicitly.
  3. Step 3: Add the rice and stir so it is coated with the aromatic oil; cook 2–3 minutes to toast it.
  4. Step 4: Start adding the hot stock gradually, stirring continuously, until the rice is cooked.
  5. Step 5: Finish by stirring in the truffle oil and the Parmesan.

Ingredients
  • 1½ CUPS WATER, JUST SLIGHTLY WARMED
  • 6 OUNCES YEAST
  • 4 CUPS ALL-PURPOSE FLOUR
  • 1 TABLESPOON SALT
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Let the yeast bloom in the warm water for 5 minutes.
  2. Step 2: In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle, combine the flour and salt.
  3. Step 3: Add the bloomed yeast mixture and mix on the lowest speed for 10 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Stop the mixer and rest the dough 10 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Raise the mixer to medium speed and mix 10 minutes more.
  6. Step 6: Set the dough aside for later use.

Preparation

  7. Step 7: Season the steaks with T-Bone Steak Dust (sub-recipe below) and sear over high heat, 4 minutes per side.
  8. Step 8: Serve the steaks with the roasted garlic cloves. (Despite the title, no separate pan-sauce steps are printed in the visible text beyond the roasted garlic and its stock/butter cooking liquid.)

SERVES 8–10 | Health Focus: Lycopene & Vegetables

Adapted from Flavors from the Farm.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A drink, not a food — enjoy occasionally; the fresh ingredients are the bright spot
  • Sardines and anchovies — small fish are the richest easy source of EPA and DHA, the omega-3 fats that help keep heart rhythm steady, calm inflammation, and build brain cells; eating the soft bones adds calcium. Small and short-lived, they also carry far less mercury than big fish.
  • Oysters — more zinc per bite than almost any food; zinc is what your immune cells are built with and it helps wounds heal. Plus B12 for red blood cells and a little omega-3.
  • The garnish is the meal's worth — the drink itself is salt and spirits; the seafood on top is genuinely nutritious.
Ingredients
  • FOR THE MIX
  • 4 cups Zing Zang Bloody Mary mix
  • ¼ cup fresh lemon juice
  • ¼ cup Worcestershire sauce
  • ¼–½ cup prepared horseradish
  • 1–10 shakes hot sauce, such as Crystal or Tabasco
  • Pinch of celery salt
  • Freshly ground black pepper
  • Small piece fresh horseradish root, peeled
  • Vodka (2–3 oz per cocktail)
  • Garnishes
  • GARNISHES
  • Pickled vegetables of any type except beets
  • Carrots, radishes, or Hakurei turnips
  • Blanched sugar snap peas
  • Little Gem leaves
  • Celery rib with frilly leaves—always
  • Cucumber spears
  • Cured meats, such as dry salami, mortadella, prosciutto cotto, country ham, jerky, or crispy bacon
  • Green chile rings, such as Anaheim or poblano
  • Crispy pepperoni
  • Olives of all types
  • Marinated cheese chunks, such as feta
  • Anchovy fillets and other tinned fish
  • Pickled peppers
  • Flowering herbs like basil, cilantro, papalo, or pipicha
  • Citrus wedges
  • Cherry tomatoes
  • Fried shallots
  • Raw oysters or other chilled seafood
Preparation
  1. Step 1: For the mix: in a large pitcher, combine the Zing Zang mix, lemon juice, Worcestershire, prepared horseradish (amount to taste/heat preference), hot sauce, celery salt, and several grinds of black pepper.
  2. Step 2: Finely grate in a little fresh horseradish, stir well, taste, and adjust seasoning; if not using right away, cover and refrigerate.
  3. Step 3: For each cocktail: fill a tall glass with ice, pour in about 4 oz of the mix and the vodka (2–3 oz), stir about 1 minute until chilled, then garnish generously.
  4. Step 4: Serve with a celery stick for stirring so settled bits are mixed back in.
Headnote (paraphrased): author favours a ready-made mix as base over homemade tomato concentrate, keeps drink fresh and simple apart from elaborate garnishes, likes it very spicy and heavily garnished, with lemon wedge and celery.
SERVES 1 | Health Focus: Botanicals

Adapted from Flavors from the Farm.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A drink, not a food — enjoy occasionally; the fresh ingredients are the bright spot
  • Egg white — pure protein foam: the texture of the drink with almost nothing else attached.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Honey — a natural sweetener with trace protective compounds; your body still treats it as sugar, so a little goes a long way.
Ingredients
  • 2 oz gin or tequila
  • 1 oz fresh lemon or lime juice
  • 1½ tablespoons runny spring honey
  • 1 large egg white
  • Dash of lavender bitters
  • Splash of club soda (about 1 oz)
  • Lavender sprig, for garnish
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a shaker, combine gin, lemon juice, honey, egg white, and bitters; cover and dry-shake vigorously at least 1 minute to build froth from the egg white.
  2. Step 2: Add a handful of ice and shake vigorously again until well chilled.
  3. Step 3: Strain into a chilled highball glass, top with club soda, and garnish with a lavender sprig.
Headnote (paraphrased): long background on growing lavender on the farm and lavender types for cooking; English lavender described as sweeter/better for culinary use than French/Spanish types.
Incomplete as photographed: photo is sideways and text is small; ingredient list and method were read from an enlarged crop, and the long headnote is only summarised, not fully transcribed.

Adapted from Flavors from the Farm.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A drink, not a food — enjoy occasionally; the fresh ingredients are the bright spot
  • A martini is alcohol, full stop — the lemon and olive are garnish, not nutrition. Enjoy it as what it is.
  • Olives — the same heart-friendly monounsaturated fat as olive oil, plus plant compounds that help protect blood vessels.
Ingredients
  • Splash of dry vermouth, for rinse
  • 2½ oz vodka or gin
  • Drop of olive brine
  • Lemon twist, for garnish
  • 2 or 3 olives, preferably Castelvetrano with pits or stuffed when in the mood, for garnish
  • 1 or 2 cocktail onions, 1 pickled chile, or 1 pickled green bean, for garnish
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Pour the vermouth splash into a well-chilled martini or Nick and Nora glass, swirl to coat the sides, and discard the excess.
  2. Step 2: In a mixing glass or shaker, combine vodka (or gin) and olive brine, fill with ice, and stir or shake (author prefers shaken) vigorously until very cold.
  3. Step 3: Strain into the prepared glass and add all the garnishes on skewers.
Headnote (paraphrased): author prefers vodka over gin, prefers shaken not stirred until very cold with fine ice crystals, and likes many garnishes rather than a single olive.

Ingredients

  • ½ teaspoon white vinegar
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Make the crust: Put flour, sugar and salt for the crust in a mixer bowl with paddle; mix briefly on medium. Add cold butter cubes one at a time until mixture looks speckled and crumbly. With mixer still running, add water and vinegar just until combined; do not overmix.
  2. Step 2: Form dough into roughly a 10×10-inch square on plastic wrap on the counter, wrap tightly in the plastic, and chill in the refrigerator overnight.
  3. Step 3: Let crust come to room temperature. Lightly flour counter and rolling pin, roll crust slightly larger than the pie pan, lay it in the pan and press gently into edges. Trim overhang and discard. Freeze crust in pan at least 15 minutes, or until ready to blind-bake.
  4. Step 4: Blind-bake: Preheat oven to 400°F. Line top of crust with foil or parchment, weigh down with dried beans or rice, and blind-bake 30 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Make filling and topping: Preheat oven to 375°F. In a medium sauté pan or skillet melt the 1 tablespoon butter, add onions and ½ teaspoon salt. Cook onions over medium-low heat about 40 minutes until deeply caramelized; if they brown too fast, add a little (about ⅛ cup) water to the pan, scrape up browned bits, and continue — yielding a scant caramelized onions.
  6. Step 6: Toss half the tomatoes with ½ teaspoon salt and ½ teaspoon sugar; set over a colander and let drain while everything else is prepared, at least [time partly obscured — minutes not legible in photo].
  7. Step 7: Toss remaining tomatoes with ½ teaspoon salt, the thyme and the olive oil. Spread in a single layer with as much separation as possible on a sheet tray. Slide tray onto middle rack and roast 20 to 30 minutes until tomatoes dry out and brown slightly.
  8. Step 8: Assemble: Stir together onions, fresh (drained) tomatoes, roasted tomatoes, remaining salt and sugar, black pepper and basil. In a separate smaller bowl stir together mayonnaise, Fontina and Parmigiano-Reggiano.
  9. Step 9: Spoon filling into blind-baked crust and top with the mayo-and-cheese mixture. Bake on middle rack 30 minutes. Serve warm or at room temperature.
Intro notes the pie is a popular seasonal item at Chef and the Farmer; using two colours of tomatoes — one colour for the roasted portion, another for the fresh — is suggested for visual effect. A store-bought crust may be used if making only the filling.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
  • Flour and butter — a crust is a vehicle. It earns its place by what it carries, and by being thin.
Ingredients
  • 1¼ cups all-purpose flour
  • 2½ teaspoons granulated sugar
  • ½ teaspoon salt
  • 6 tablespoons cold butter cut into ½-inch cubes
  • 2 tablespoons ice-cold water
  • ½ teaspoon white vinegar
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Sub-recipe belonging to Roasted and Fresh Tomato Pie — method is steps 1–4 of that recipe: mix dry ingredients, cut in cold butter, add water and vinegar just to combine, shape, wrap and chill overnight, roll out, fit to pan, trim, freeze at least 15 minutes, then blind-bake at 400°F for 30 minutes weighted with beans or rice.

Serves 4 | Health Focus: Vitamin K & Calcium

Adapted from Deep Run Roots.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Collard greens — vitamin K and calcium for strong bones, plus fiber; dark greens like these pack more nutrition per calorie than almost anything else.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
  • Ham hock — here it's the seasoning, not the serving: a little smoked pork flavors a whole pot of greens, which is the traditional trade — big flavor, modest meat.
Ingredients
  • 1 ham hock or 8 to 10 ounces other pork seasoning meat
  • 3 quarts of water
  • 1 medium yellow onion, diced
  • ½ teaspoon red chili flakes
  • 10 turns of the pepper mill or ¼ teaspoon black pepper
  • 2 pounds or 1 whole head collards, large stems removed
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 1 tablespoon granulated sugar (optional)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a 6- to 8-quart Dutch oven or pot combine ham hock/seasoning meat, water, onion, chili flakes and black pepper. Cover, bring to a boil, and cook covered 30 minutes.
  2. Step 2: Add collards, lower heat to a heavy simmer, cover and cook 1½ hours.
  3. Step 3: Remove lid and check for doneness — greens should have absorbed pork flavour from the broth and be silky-soft.
  4. Step 4: Scoop greens into a bowl, leaving pot liquor behind. Pick the smoked meat from the hock or chop the seasoning meat into rough pieces and add to the greens.
  5. Step 5: Roughly chop greens and meat together using a collard chopper or knife, to your preferred texture. Stir in up to 1 teaspoon salt and 1 tablespoon sugar if judged necessary.
  6. Step 6: Skim the white foam/fat (called "shine" in the intro) off the top of the pot liquor and stir it into the greens.
  7. Step 7: Serve greens warm with hot sauce or hot pepper vinegar. Reserve pot liquor for another use or drink it.
Intro discusses family/traditional approaches to collards and notes the white foamy fat on the pot liquor ("shine") is prized and stirred in rather than discarded.
Serves 3 or 4 | Oven: 400°F | Health Focus: Protein & Vitamin C

Adapted from Deep Run Roots.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Peaches — vitamin C for immune system and skin, plus beta-carotene your body turns into vitamin A for your eyes. The skin carries fiber, so unpeeled keeps more.
  • Chicken — lean, complete protein: all the building blocks for keeping muscle, without much fat, especially with the skin off. Wings and drumsticks with the skin and glaze are richer than plain breast meat — the protein is real, and so is the sweet coating; the glaze is a few spoonfuls over the whole tray, not a bath.
Ingredients
  • 12 to 14 chicken wings or 10 drumsticks
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
  • 1 tablespoon salt
  • ⅔ cup Jalapeño Peach Glaze
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Make the Jalapeño Peach Glaze first (see separate sub-recipe entry below).
  2. Step 2: Cook the chicken: Preheat oven to 400°F and let chicken come to room temperature. Toss chicken with the oil and salt and spread in a single layer on a baking sheet, pieces not touching so they brown evenly.
  3. Step 3: Place tray on middle rack and roast undisturbed 10 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Remove from oven, stir/turn the pieces in the pan, and cook an additional 10 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Remove again, pour off any accumulated fat, and toss pieces with the glaze/sauce. Return tray to oven and roast an additional 15 minutes, until caramelized in places and shiny in others.
Intro says the wings/drums are roasted and finished in the oven with glaze, but could equally be cooked on the grill with sauce applied at the same time for caramelization. The glaze is described as a base for vinaigrettes, a sauce for poultry or pork, and a companion for creamy cheeses; a big batch can be refrigerated up to three months or jarred and processed in a hot-water bath canner for ten minutes (page 16).
Makes 5 cups (sub-recipe for Jalapeño Peach Chicken) | Health Focus: Vitamin C & Capsaicin

Adapted from Deep Run Roots.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Ginger — its bite comes from gingerol, which helps calm nausea and queasiness and eases everyday inflammation. That's why ginger settles a stomach.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Peaches — vitamin C for immune system and skin, plus beta-carotene your body turns into vitamin A for your eyes. The skin carries fiber, so unpeeled keeps more.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
  • It carries real sugar — that's what makes it a glaze. The fruit and chiles are genuine; the sugar is too.
Ingredients
  • 3 cups chopped peach, about 4–5 medium peaches
  • 1 pound jalapeños, stemmed and seeded
  • ½ onion, roughly chopped
  • 2 tablespoons ginger, peeled and roughly chopped
  • 1¼ cups cider vinegar
  • 2¼ cups granulated sugar
  • 1 teaspoon salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Put peaches, jalapeños, onion and ginger in a food processor and pulse until shredded and juicy but not fully puréed.
  2. Step 2: Transfer the chunky mixture to a 4- to 6-quart Dutch oven and add vinegar, sugar and salt. Over medium heat bring to a boil, skimming off foam that rises as often as possible — less foam boiled back in gives a clearer glaze.
  3. Step 3: Cook at a medium simmer about 30 minutes; it should thicken slightly but not look darkened in colour.
  4. Step 4: After 30 minutes test consistency: pour a little on a chilled plate, slide the plate into the fridge for 5 minutes; if it runs like heavy cream when the plate is tilted, cook longer, and if it pools/drips like loose honey it is ready.
See storage/serving notes under Jalapeño Peach Chicken (refrigerate up to three months, or can in a hot-water bath for ten minutes).
MAKES 2 CUPS | Health Focus: Healthy Fats & Plant Protein

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Garlic, raw — raw garlic keeps all of its allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. Crush it and give it a few minutes before eating — that's when the allicin forms.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Ginger — its bite comes from gingerol, which helps calm nausea and queasiness and eases everyday inflammation. That's why ginger settles a stomach.
  • Peanuts — plant protein plus monounsaturated fat, the heart-friendly kind; the combination keeps you full for a long time.
Ingredients
  • ½ cup soy sauce
  • ½ cup rice wine vinegar
  • ½ cup chunky peanut butter
  • ⅓ cup chopped cilantro
  • 2 tablespoons dark honey
  • 1 tablespoon toasted sesame oil
  • 1 tablespoon freshly grated ginger
  • Zest and juice of 1 lime
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • ½ teaspoon red pepper flakes
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Stir all ingredients together until well mixed.
  2. Step 2: To use as a marinade, pour over meat or vegetables and marinate 30 to 60 minutes in the refrigerator.
  3. Step 3: To serve as a dipping sauce, refrigerate until ready to serve.
Intro recommends serving with raw or grilled vegetables (asparagus, zucchini sticks, red pepper strips, carrots, broccoli) and pita chips, using it as a marinade for vegetables, poultry, pork, fish and shellfish, and notes it pairs with Grilled Baby Bok Choy with Fresh Ginger-Soy Sauce (page 122).

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic, raw — raw garlic keeps all of its allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. Crush it and give it a few minutes before eating — that's when the allicin forms.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • 1 cup olive oil
  • 1 cup sherry vinegar
  • 1 cup chopped flat-leaf parsley
  • ¼ cup chopped fresh oregano
  • ¼ cup chopped yellow onion (1 small onion)
  • 6 garlic cloves, minced
  • 2 teaspoons cayenne pepper
  • 1 teaspoon black pepper
  • ½ teaspoon sea salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Stir all ingredients together until well mixed.
  2. Step 2: Store in a glass jar in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.
Intro describes it as a traditional Argentinian marinade, versatile as a side sauce (e.g. with Grilled Turkey Breast over Winter Greens with Warm Cranberry Vinaigrette, page 142) and drizzled as a finishing sauce over grilled vegetable platters, pasta, fish, beef, poultry, and French-Style Grilled Potato Salad (page 115).

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • 1 tablespoon finely chopped fresh rosemary
  • ½ teaspoon fine kosher or sea salt
  • 2 garlic cloves, minced
  • ½ cup olive oil
  • Zest and juice of 1 lemon
  • Freshly ground black pepper to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Mortar-and-pestle method: Grind rosemary, salt and garlic together in the mortar to a fine paste. Drizzle in olive oil and grind again. Add lemon zest and juice, grind, taste, and add more salt if wanted and season with pepper.
  2. Step 2: Food-processor alternative: Pulse rosemary, salt and garlic just until chopped into a paste. Add olive oil and pulse again. Add lemon zest and juice and pulse, then season with salt and pepper as needed.
  3. Step 3: Keeps in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.
Intro describes it as looser than a paste — a basting sauce/drizzle for garden vegetables, beef, pork, chicken or leg of lamb before, during and after grilling; suggested on High-Heat Grilled Romaine Salad (page 109), brushed on bread or pizza dough, and drizzled over grilled asparagus, greens and tomatoes. A mortar and pestle is recommended for best texture; a food processor may also be used.

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
  • It's butter — a rich finishing sauce. A spoonful over something lean is the balance.
Ingredients
  • 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter, at room temperature
  • 2 tablespoons chopped shallots
  • 1 tablespoon white wine vinegar
  • 2 tablespoons chopped fresh tarragon leaves
  • ¼ teaspoon sea salt
  • ½ teaspoon hot sauce or to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a medium bowl stir all ingredients together with a fork.
  2. Step 2: Either spoon into a ramekin or small bowl for serving, or shape into a roll, wrap in waxed paper, and chill.
  3. Step 3: For freezer storage up to 3 months, wrap tightly first in waxed paper, then in layers of plastic wrap and aluminum foil.
Intro suggests spreading on a bread crouton to top Smoked Tomato Bisque (page 128), adding pats to Grilled Spring Platter of Asparagus and Leeks (page 161), and serving at room temperature with grill-roasted potatoes (page 8), grilled bread, asparagus, poultry or steaks. The recipe halves easily; the extra half can be labelled, dated and frozen ready for use.

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Edamame — young soybeans are a rare snack with both protein and fiber: protein to build with, fiber that feeds gut bacteria and slows digestion so you stay full.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
Ingredients
  • 1 pound fresh edamame in the pod
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
  • 2 teaspoons toasted sesame oil
  • Flaked salt for serving
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat grill to medium-high. In a large bowl toss edamame pods with both oils.
  2. Step 2: Put pods on a perforated grill rack or in a disposable aluminum pan, arranged in a single layer on the grill over medium-high heat. Grill-roast (page 8), covered, 4 to 5 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Flip, cover, and grill a few minutes more, until pods are crisp-tender when pierced with a knife. If unsure, remove a pod, open it and taste a bean to check.
  4. Step 4: To eat, tear open the pods and dip the beans into flaked salt.
Headnote says edamame meant for fresh eating can be grilled right in the pod and served on a platter with a small dish of flaked salt. A separate "GROWING EDAMAME" box gives growing notes in paraphrase: edamame is the Japanese name for soybeans eaten fresh; plant like green beans after frost danger, seeds in full sun about 1 inch deep and 2 inches apart, can be grown in large pots around a wire frame/trellis, best in spring or fall as a cool-weather crop; about 3 soybeans per pod, pick when beans within the pod are young and tender, about ½ inch long.

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Bok choy — calcium for bones and vitamin A for eyes and immune system, in a green so light it's mostly water and crunch.
  • Ginger — its bite comes from gingerol, which helps calm nausea and queasiness and eases everyday inflammation. That's why ginger settles a stomach.
Ingredients
  • 2 small heads bok choy, trimmed and halved lengthwise
  • FRESH GINGER SOY SAUCE
  • ¼ cup (½ stick) unsalted butter, melted
  • 2 tablespoons olive oil
  • 2 teaspoons soy sauce
  • 2 teaspoons fresh ginger, minced
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Prepare a medium-hot fire in the grill. Rinse bok choy, drain well, and pat dry.
  2. Step 2: Make the Ginger-Soy Sauce (see separate sub-recipe entry below): whisk together melted butter, olive oil, soy sauce, ginger and garlic.
  3. Step 3: Brush bok choy with the sauce and place cut side down directly over the fire. Grill about 10 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Baste the leaves, turn, and continue grilling about another 10 minutes until bok choy is fork-tender.
  5. Step 5: Serve with any remaining sauce.
Intro notes late spring/early summer dwarf bok choy heads (also called pak choi) are tender and sweet, the sturdy leafy stalks suit breaking apart and serving with a dipping sauce such as Satay-Style Peanut Dipping Sauce (page 23), and the Fresh Ginger-Soy sauce is versatile — try it with grilled asparagus, eggplant and zucchini.

Adapted from The Gardener & the Grill.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Corn — fiber for digestion, plus lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
Ingredients
  • 6 ears sweet corn, in the husk
  • 1 garlic clove, minced
  • ¼ cup (½ stick) unsalted butter, at room temperature
  • ½ teaspoon ground ancho chile powder
  • ½ teaspoon grated lime zest
  • Fine kosher or sea salt to taste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Peel husks back without detaching them, remove the corn silk, then pull husks back over the corn and tie them securely closed with kitchen string or a strip of corn husk. Soak corn in cold water 15 minutes; drain well.
  2. Step 2: Make the Ancho-Lime Butter (see separate sub-recipe entry below): stir garlic, butter, ancho chile and lime zest together in a bowl until well blended; add salt to taste and set aside.
  3. Step 3: Prepare a hot fire in the grill.
  4. Step 4: Grill corn directly over the heat, turning often, about 10 minutes, until husks are slightly charred and steam rises from the ears. Let cool slightly and remove the string.
  5. Step 5: To serve, pull husks back and brush kernels with the Ancho-Lime Butter.
Intro says grilling in the husk keeps sweet corn very tender while giving a gentle grill flavour; varieties suggested include Silver Queen, Purdue Super Sweet, Peaches and Cream, and the heirloom Country Gentleman.

Adapted from Salt & Shore.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Shrimp — lean protein for very few calories, plus selenium, a mineral your thyroid needs to make its hormones and your cells need to defend themselves.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.

Ingredients
  • 4 tablespoons salted butter
  • 1/4 cup Peanut Chile Crisp or a mix of store-bought chile crisp and finely chopped peanuts
  • 1 lb large shrimp (preferably from Sun Shrimp), peeled and deveined
  • Kosher salt
  • 1/2 cup finely chopped fresh cilantro
  • 1 lime
  • Crusty bread slices, for serving (optional)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat a large cast-iron skillet, Dutch oven, or sauté pan over medium heat for 3 minutes.
  2. Step 2: Add butter, chile crisp, and shrimp; stir until well mixed.
  3. Step 3: Season lightly with salt and cook, stirring somewhat frequently, 3–5 minutes until shrimp are cooked.
  4. Step 4: Remove from heat and fold in cilantro.
  5. Step 5: Spoon into a cazuela, cocotte, or serving bowl, grate lime zest directly over the dish, and serve.
Intro notes the dish is inspired by Spanish gambas al ajillo, balances spicy/buttery/citrus, peanuts add depth; quick and easy, traditionally enjoyed pinchos-style skewered with toothpicks; Florida-based Sun Shrimp (p. 88) preferred when possible. Serving note: delightful as is, sometimes served with crusty bread for dipping.

  • 1 tablespoon firmly packed organic dark brown sugar

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Tomatoes — lycopene, the red pigment, helps protect the heart and blood vessels, and cooking tomatoes in a little oil makes it much easier for your body to absorb: one case where cooked beats raw.
Ingredients
  • 4 boneless beef sirloin steaks, at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick, trimmed of excess fat
  • Salt
  • 1 tablespoon cracked black peppercorns
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • FOR THE PAN SAUCE:
  • 1 tablespoon unsalted butter
  • 1/2 red onion, finely chopped
  • 1 clove garlic, minced
  • 1/2 cup (4 fl oz/125 ml) dry red wine
  • 1 cup (8 fl oz/250 ml) beef stock (page 110) or prepared broth, plus more if needed
  • 1 tablespoon tomato paste
  • 1 tablespoon cornstarch (cornflour) combined with 2 tablespoons water
  • 2 tablespoons chopped fresh flat-leaf (Italian) parsley
  • Salt and freshly ground pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Slash edges of steaks in 1 or 2 places to prevent curling. Sprinkle all sides generously with salt and cracked black pepper, pressing pepper into the surface. Let stand at room temperature at least 15 minutes and up to 1 hour before cooking.
  2. Step 2: In a large, heavy frying pan over medium-high heat, heat olive oil. Add steaks and cook to desired doneness, turning once, 3–5 minutes on each side. Test with an instant-read thermometer or by cutting into the meat. Remove steaks when they are red at the center for rare (120°F/49°C) or deep pink at the center for medium-rare (130°F/54°C). Transfer to a platter, tent loosely with aluminum foil, and rest while making the pan sauce.
  3. Step 3: Pan sauce: In the same frying pan over medium-high heat, melt butter. Add onion and garlic and sauté until onion is softened, 3–5 minutes. Add wine and stock and boil until reduced by half, 4–5 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Reduce heat to medium, whisk in tomato paste and cornstarch mixture, and simmer, whisking occasionally, until slightly thickened, 3–5 minutes. Add more stock if sauce seems too thick. Stir in parsley and season to taste with salt and pepper.
  5. Step 5: To serve, spoon a generous amount of sauce over steaks and serve at once; pass extra sauce at the table.
Sidebar "MAKING PAN SAUCES" (paraphrased): To make a sauce in the pan used to cook meat, first add a little olive oil and sauté minced garlic or shallot, then pour in wine, stock, or another liquid to deglaze, scraping up browned bits. Next stir in seasonings such as herbs, mustard, tomato paste, Worcestershire sauce, or soy sauce. Thicken by reducing over high heat or by stirring in a little cornstarch mixed with water and cooking a few minutes longer. For a richer sauce, stir in 2 tablespoons heavy (double) cream or chilled unsalted butter at the end.
MAKES 8–10 SERVINGS | Oven: 350°F (180°C) | Health Focus: Iron, B12 & Protein

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Beef and lamb — iron in the form your body absorbs best, plus vitamin B12, which you need to make red blood cells and keep nerves working; running low leaves you tired and foggy.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
  • Prime rib is the celebration cut — marbled and rich. The horseradish crust is the smart part: huge flavor for almost no calories.
Ingredients
  • FOR THE CRUST:
  • 1/2 cup (4 oz/125 g) Dijon mustard
  • 1/4 cup (2 oz/60 g) prepared horseradish
  • 1/4 cup (3 oz/90 g) dried bread crumbs
  • 2 tablespoons chopped fresh rosemary or 1 tablespoon dried
  • 6 cloves garlic, minced
  • 2 teaspoons salt
  • 2 teaspoons freshly ground pepper
  • 1 standing prime rib roast (4 ribs), 6–8 lb (3–4 kg), chine bone removed by the butcher
  • 1/2 cup (4 oz/125 g) prepared horseradish
  • 1/2 cup (4 oz/125 g) sour cream
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Crust: In a small bowl, mix mustard, 1/4 cup horseradish, bread crumbs, rosemary, garlic, salt, and pepper. Rub mixture all over the meat and let stand at room temperature for at least 15 minutes or up to 1 hour, or cover and refrigerate overnight; bring to room temperature, if necessary, before cooking.
  2. Step 2: Preheat oven to 350°F (180°C). Oil a roasting pan just large enough to hold the roast. Place rib roast fat side up in the pan and roast until nicely browned, about 1 hour. Check doneness with an instant-read thermometer inserted away from the bone or by cutting into meat near the bone: for rare beef remove roast at 120°–125°F (49°–52°C) when meat is red near the bone; for medium-rare remove at 130°F (54°C) when meat is deep pink near the bone.
  3. Step 3: Transfer roast to a carving board and let rest, tented loosely with aluminum foil, for 10–12 minutes before serving.
  4. Step 4: Whisk 1/2 cup horseradish and sour cream together in a small bowl. Carve roast (left) into thick or thin slices as desired, transfer to individual plates, and serve with horseradish sauce on top.
Sidebar "CARVING RIB ROASTS" (paraphrased): Carving prime rib, bone-in pork loin, and racks of lamb is easier when the butcher removes the chine bone that runs along the bottom. To carve, place roast on a carving board holding the knife parallel to the ribs, slice along the edge of the ribs under the rib-eye (the meaty portion) to separate it from the bones, then slice the rib-eye as thinly or thickly as liked; or cut between the bones for bone-in slices. Variation Tip (paraphrased): Rib roast can also be cooked on a grill — prepare a charcoal or gas grill for indirect grilling over medium-high heat (p. 106), place prepared roast fat side up over the cooler portion with a drip pan underneath, cover, and roast for 1 hour; check doneness as directed above.
MAKES 4–6 SERVINGS | Oven: 450°F (230°C) | Health Focus: Iron, B12 & Protein

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Beef and lamb — iron in the form your body absorbs best, plus vitamin B12, which you need to make red blood cells and keep nerves working; running low leaves you tired and foggy.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • 2 racks of lamb, about 1 1/2 lb (750 g) each, frenched by the butcher
  • Salt and freshly ground pepper
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
  • FOR THE CRUST:
  • 1/2 cup (2 oz/60 g) dried bread crumbs
  • 2 teaspoons finely chopped fresh rosemary
  • 2 teaspoons garlic powder or granulated garlic
  • 1/4 cup (2 fl oz/60 ml) olive oil, or as needed
  • 2 tablespoons Dijon mustard
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Season lamb generously with salt and pepper. Let meat stand at room temperature at least 15 minutes or up to 1 hour before cooking.
  2. Step 2: Preheat oven to 450°F (230°C).
  3. Step 3: In a large ovenproof frying pan over medium-high heat, heat olive oil. When oil starts to smoke, add racks fat side down. Sear until golden brown on all sides, about 2 minutes on each side; do not crowd the pan (use 2 frying pans if necessary). When browned, transfer to a platter and set aside to cool. Reserve the pan(s).
  4. Step 4: Crust: In a bowl, combine bread crumbs, rosemary, and garlic powder and mix well. Add olive oil until bread crumbs have the feel of wet sand; you may need more or less than 1/4 cup. Using a spatula, spread mustard over the meat of each rack, excluding the bones. Pack bread crumb mixture over the mustard to help it adhere.
  5. Step 5: Return racks to the pan(s) and roast in the oven until an instant-read thermometer inserted away from the bone registers 130°F (54°C) and meat is quite pink when cut into near the bone for medium-rare, 12–15 minutes.
  6. Step 6: Transfer to a carving board and let rest, loosely tented with aluminum foil, for 5–10 minutes before serving.
  7. Step 7: Carve into chops and serve 2 to each diner.
Sidebar "PAN-ROASTING" (paraphrased): Pan-roasting involves browning meat on the stovetop then finishing it by roasting in a hot oven. In a restaurant this allows the chef to precook the meat then finish it quickly with a brief final roasting. For home cooks it offers partially cooking the roast ahead of time while ensuring a browned surface and perfectly cooked interior. For more on roasting, see p. 109.
MAKES 2 quarts | Health Focus: Whole Grains & Fiber

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Corn — fiber for digestion, plus lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age.
  • Popcorn — a true whole grain with real fiber that fills you up, as long as it isn't drowned in butter and salt.
Ingredients
  • 1/4 cup popcorn kernels, preferably an heirloom variety
  • 1/4 cup olive oil
  • 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard
  • 1/4 teaspoon sea salt
  • Black pepper in a mill
  • 1/4 cup finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Place popcorn kernels in a paper lunch bag and fold over the top three times in 1-inch folds. Place upright in the microwave for 1 minute 45 seconds, or until popping slows to 3 to 5 seconds between each pop.
  2. Step 2: In a large bowl, combine olive oil, mustard, salt, and about 40 cranks of the pepper mill. Whisk together (it will not entirely emulsify), then use a rubber spatula to spread the mixture around the sides of the bowl (it will thicken into a paste as spread).
  3. Step 3: Add popcorn to the bowl and use a spatula to fold popcorn against the coated walls; make sure popcorn is well coated.
  4. Step 4: Add cheese in three batches, using hands to incorporate each addition before adding more. Serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): Popcorn described as an all-occasion food; author prefers heirloom varieties such as Indigo or Yellow Flint from Geechie Boy Mill for distinctive flavor; recipe has few ingredients so use best quality available but can be adapted to what is on hand; as a snack it feeds 2 really hungry skiers or 4 to 6 people with normal appetites.
MAKES 48 oysters | Oven: 400°F convection (425°F regular oven) | Health Focus: Zinc & Omega-3s

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Oysters — more zinc per bite than almost any food; zinc is what your immune cells are built with and it helps wounds heal. Plus B12 for red blood cells and a little omega-3.
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Tomatoes — lycopene, the red pigment, helps protect the heart and blood vessels, and cooking tomatoes in a little oil makes it much easier for your body to absorb: one case where cooked beats raw.
  • Corn — fiber for digestion, plus lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
Ingredients
  • 1/2 cup Roasted Tomatoes (page 162), minced
  • 1/2 teaspoon minced shallot
  • 2 tablespoons olive oil
  • Black pepper in a mill
  • Sea salt
  • 2 tablespoons neutral vegetable oil
  • 1/2 cup minced yellow onion
  • 10 ounces turnip greens (about 1 bunch), roughly chopped
  • 1/2 cup heavy cream
  • 1 cup finely diced turnip root
  • 4 dozen chubby East Coast oysters, on the half shell
  • 1/4 cup cornbread crumbs (see page 100)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Tomato relish: In a small bowl, combine tomatoes, shallot, olive oil, 10 cranks of the pepper mill, and 1/4 teaspoon salt. Set aside.
  2. Step 2: In a large, heavy-bottomed skillet, heat oil over medium heat. Add onion and cook until softened, about 3 minutes. Add turnip greens and cook, stirring occasionally, until greens are tender, about 4 minutes. Season with salt and remove from heat. When greens are cool enough to handle, squeeze out excess moisture; set aside.
  3. Step 3: In a small saucepan over medium heat, combine cream, 1/4 teaspoon salt, diced turnip root, and 1/2 cup water and bring to a simmer. Reduce heat to low and simmer until turnip is tender, about 12 minutes. Transfer cream and turnip mixture to a food processor and pulse until it forms a paste. Add reserved turnip greens and puree for 60 to 90 seconds. Taste and season to the salt level of the oysters (see Note). Set aside.
  4. Step 4: Preheat a convection oven to 400°F (or a regular oven to 425°F). Cover two rimmed baking sheets with a layer of rock salt to serve as a bed for the oysters. Arrange oysters in their half shells on the rock salt. Season oysters lightly with salt, then top each with 1 teaspoon of the creamed turnip greens.
  5. Step 5: Transfer oysters to the oven and bake for 6 to 8 minutes, until oysters just start to bubble around the edges.
  6. Step 6: Top each oyster with 1/2 teaspoon of the tomato relish and a pinch of cornbread crumbs. Serve immediately.
Note printed with ingredients: If oysters are super briny, avoid adding extra salt. Method note: Creamed turnip greens can be made up to 3 days in advance and stored in the refrigerator until ready to use. Intro (paraphrased): Inspired by oysters Rockefeller and Carolina coast oyster bars; best enjoyed straight from the oven with a can of ice-cold beer-flavored beer.
SERVES 8 | Health Focus: Folate & B Vitamins

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Mushrooms — deep savory flavor for very few calories, plus B vitamins your body uses to turn food into energy.
  • Asparagus — folate for making new cells, plus inulin, a fiber your good gut bacteria feed on (that's what 'prebiotic' means).
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
Ingredients
  • 3 tablespoons neutral vegetable oil
  • 2 pounds oyster mushrooms, tough stems removed, torn into bite-size pieces
  • Sea salt
  • 1/4 cup minced shallots
  • 4 thyme sprigs
  • 2 pounds asparagus, ends trimmed and cut into 2-inch pieces
  • 1 cup amontillado sherry (I like Lustau)
  • 3/4 cup heavy cream
  • 2 tablespoons cold unsalted butter, cut into cubes
  • 2 tablespoons Porcini Butter (page 20)
  • Juice of 1/2 lemon
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a large skillet, heat oil over medium heat. Add mushrooms and let sear, stirring a few times, until moisture they release has evaporated and edges begin to crisp and caramelize. Season lightly with salt.
  2. Step 2: Add shallots and thyme and cook for 1 minute, stirring to combine and coat everything. Stir in asparagus, then add sherry and deglaze the pan by swirling and scraping the bottom to release browned bits. Cook until liquid is reduced by three-quarters, stirring occasionally, about 3 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Add cream and let it reduce until slightly thickened and coating the asparagus and mushrooms, about another 2 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in the cold butters.
  4. Step 4: Stir in lemon juice, season with salt to taste, and serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): Oyster mushrooms described as meaty, mild, buttery; mushrooms hold moisture so season with salt after searing to let liquid evaporate, ensuring caramelization before tossing with sherry and cream.
SERVES 6 to 8 | Health Focus: Potassium

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Potatoes — potassium, which helps keep blood pressure in check by balancing salt, plus filling starch that keeps you full. Much of the fiber is in the skin, so skin-on keeps more of it.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
  • Cream is the comfort here — the potatoes and herbs are the substance.
Ingredients
  • 4 cups heavy cream
  • 1 1/2 teaspoons black peppercorns
  • 1/2 shallot
  • 1 head garlic, halved across the equator
  • 1 fresh bay leaf
  • 4 thyme sprigs
  • 2 pounds Yukon gold potatoes
  • 2 pounds russet potatoes
  • Kosher salt
  • 1 cup unsalted butter, cut into cubes, at room temperature
  • Sea salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a large saucepan over medium heat, bring cream, peppercorns, shallot, garlic, and bay leaf to a boil. Remove from heat and add thyme. Let steep for 15 minutes. Strain cream through a fine-mesh sieve, discarding solids and reserving cream.
  2. Step 2: Peel potatoes and cut into 1-inch cubes. Place potatoes in a pot with 10 cups water and season with 2 tablespoons kosher salt. Place pot over high heat and bring to a boil. Reduce to a simmer and cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until potatoes are fork-tender. Drain potatoes well and return to the pot.
  3. Step 3: In a large saucepan, warm cream but do not boil. Place pot of potatoes over low heat just to warm through. Using an electric mixer, whip potatoes on medium speed until smooth. Add half of warm cream to potatoes, followed by half of butter. Continue to beat with mixer, and when both are fully incorporated, continue to add remaining cream and butter bit by bit until a silky-smooth consistency is reached; you may not need all cream and butter, depending on starchiness of potatoes.
  4. Step 4: Season potatoes with 1 teaspoon sea salt or to taste and serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): Cream is scented with aromatics so mashed potatoes move from canvas to foreground; gravy is welcome but author suggests these potatoes do not need it.
SERVES 6 to 8 | Oven: 350°F (oil temperature) | Health Focus: Quercetin & Prebiotics

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
  • Fried is fried — a crunchy treat. Baking or the air fryer keeps the onions and loses most of the oil.
Ingredients
  • 4 Vidalia or other sweet onions
  • 3 cups all-purpose flour
  • 1 cup cornstarch
  • 2 tablespoons sea salt
  • 1 tablespoon freshly ground black pepper
  • Neutral vegetable oil, for frying
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Trim tip and tail of each onion, then cut onions into fat 1/4- to 1-inch-thick rings crosswise (across the equator). Break onion slices into their natural rings, discarding centers.
  2. Step 2: Mix flour, cornstarch, salt, and pepper in a large bowl. Line a baking sheet with two or three layers of paper towels.
  3. Step 3: Fill a heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven with 3 to 4 inches of oil and set over high heat until oil reaches 350°F on a deep-fry thermometer.
  4. Step 4: Dredge onion rings in flour mixture, coating well. Transfer in batches to the pot and fry until golden brown, flipping occasionally, 5 to 6 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Transfer to prepared baking sheet and season with sea salt. Serve with choice of condiment (author notes a preference for Basic Malt Mayo on p. 21).
Intro (paraphrased): Best onion rings are imperfect, barely holding a simple batter of seasoned flour and cornstarch bound by a splash of buttermilk; mismatched ring size allows varied thickness/crunch; suggested as a starter at a gathering or served on the table as a side dish.
SERVES 4 | Health Focus: Calcium & Protein

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
  • Macaroni and cheese sauce — comfort food, and it doesn't pretend otherwise. Real cheese and milk, eaten as the rich dish it is.
Ingredients
  • Kosher salt
  • 6 ounces dry elbow macaroni (about 1 1/4 cups)
  • 1 teaspoon neutral vegetable oil
  • 2 ounces grana padano, shredded
  • 2 ounces Jarlsberg, shredded
  • 6 ounces white cheddar, shredded
  • 2 cups heavy cream
  • Sea salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a medium saucepan, bring 2 quarts water and 1 1/2 tablespoons kosher salt to a boil. Add macaroni and return to a boil; once boiling, cook until barely al dente (about 5 minutes), then drain pasta well. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet and mix in oil to keep noodles from sticking. Let cool completely; yield should be about 3 cups.
  2. Step 2: Set a rack in the oven about 4 inches from the broiler and preheat broiler. Combine grana padano, Jarlsberg, and white cheddar in a large bowl; reserve 60 percent of cheese for the top.
  3. Step 3: In a large deep saucepan, bring cream and 1 teaspoon sea salt to a boil. Let simmer for about 2 minutes; cream will foam up then subside into a simmer. Add noodles and cook, stirring occasionally, about 90 seconds; cream will start to thicken slightly and coat noodles.
  4. Step 4: Start adding 40 percent of cheese in small handfuls, stirring and waiting for each addition to melt and incorporate before adding more.
  5. Step 5: Transfer contents of pan to a 2 1/2-quart skillet or baking dish, mound reserved cheese over top, and place dish on a baking sheet to catch drips. Place baking sheet under broiler for 3 to 5 minutes, rotating throughout, until cheese melts and caramelizes into a golden-brown crust; watch carefully as broilers differ.
  6. Step 6: Remove gratin from oven and let rest 5 minutes. Serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased, long): Macaroni au Gratin is Poole's mac and cheese, made to order with reduced cream, slightly al dente elbows, three cheeses (Jarlsberg, grana padano, sharp white Vermont cheddar), and sea salt; topped cheese is broiled to a caramelized crisp. Described as a signature, most-ordered dish and a representation of the restaurant's cooking goals.
SERVES 4 | Oven: 300°F convection (325°F regular) to start, then raised to 450°F convection (475°F regular) | Health Focus: Protein & Allicin

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Chicken — lean, complete protein: all the building blocks for keeping muscle, without much fat, especially with the skin off.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • Kosher salt
  • 3 tablespoons sugar
  • 1 (3½-pound) whole chicken, quartered, backbones and wingtips removed (reserve these for making stock later)
  • 2 tablespoons neutral vegetable oil
  • 1 head garlic, halved across the equator
  • 2 rosemary sprigs
  • 4 thyme sprigs
  • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter
  • Juice of ½ lemon
  • 1 tablespoon olive oil
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Make brine: in a large pot stir 6 tablespoons salt, the sugar, and 4 cups water until dissolved; add 4 more cups cold water, add the chicken pieces, cover and refrigerate 8 to 12 hours. Lift chicken out, discard brine, pat pieces dry.
  2. Step 2: Put a rack in the bottom third of the oven and preheat to 300°F convection (325°F regular). Heat the vegetable oil in a large cast-iron skillet over medium heat until it shimmers.
  3. Step 3: Season chicken lightly with salt, lay pieces skin-side down in the skillet with as much skin touching the pan as possible; cook 1 minute, then add the garlic halves cut-side down plus the rosemary and thyme. Sear until herbs and garlic are very aromatic, about 4 to 5 minutes, then move the herbs and garlic on top of the chicken pieces so they do not burn but still flavour the chicken. Keep cooking until the skin is very crisp — lifting a piece to peek — about 3 more minutes .
  4. Step 4: Cut the butter into four equal pieces and put one piece on top of each chicken piece.
  5. Step 5: Move the pan to the oven and cook 30 minutes. Flip the chicken and raise the oven to 450°F convection (475°F regular); cook about 10 minutes more, watching closely so it does not brown too fast. Take the skillet out and move the chicken, skin-side up, to a wire rack; rest at least 10 minutes.
  6. Step 6: Take the herbs and garlic out of the skillet (the roasted garlic cloves can be used as a garnish) and pour the pan drippings into a small saucepan. After the chicken has rested 10 minutes, bring the saucepan to a simmer over medium heat, turn off the heat, and whisk in the lemon juice and olive oil.
  7. Step 7: Put the chicken on a platter, drizzle with the pan sauce, garnish with the garlic cloves if liked, and serve.
Intro (paraphrased): author presents simple roast chicken as a favourite last-meal dish, inspired by the roast chicken for two at Zuni Café in San Francisco; roast chicken is also a regular at Poole's, where a longer, slower roast is used at home to get crisp skin and tender flesh.
SERVES 6 | Oven: 450°F convection (475°F regular) to start, then reduced to 250°F convection (275°F regular) | Health Focus: Iron & Slow Cooking

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Garlic — a long simmer takes out most of its allicin, so here it's mostly the deep, mellow flavor; a little fresh crushed garlic stirred in at the end is where the health side lives.
  • Beef and lamb — iron in the form your body absorbs best, plus vitamin B12, which you need to make red blood cells and keep nerves working; running low leaves you tired and foggy.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
  • Two ingredients' worth of honesty: rich meat, simply cooked. The simplicity is the virtue; the richness is the price.
Ingredients
  • 5 pounds bone-in beef short rib slab
  • Sea salt
  • Black pepper in a mill
  • 2 cups red wine
  • 1 head garlic, halved across the equator
  • 8 thyme sprigs
  • 4 rosemary sprigs
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat convection oven to 450°F (regular oven to 475°F).
  2. Step 2: Coat the short ribs well on all sides with salt and pepper. Put them in a large roasting pan and roast 20 minutes, until a caramelized crust forms. Take the pan out and lower the oven to 250°F convection (275°F regular).
  3. Step 3: Let the ribs rest 10 minutes, then pour the wine and 2 cups water into the bottom of the pan. Add the garlic halves, thyme, and rosemary to the pan. Cover the pan tightly with foil and return to the oven.
  4. Step 4: Roast 4 hours, until the ribs are very tender but not falling apart. Remove from the oven and turn up the corners of the foil while keeping the pan mostly covered, so residual heat escapes gradually and the ribs keep most of their juices. Rest 20 minutes.
  5. Step 5: To serve: either slice between the bones and divide among plates, or cut the whole slab off the bone and cut it into 1-inch-thick slices.
Intro (paraphrased): a dead-simple method the authors settled on after trying searing/braising and grilling; the meat is versatile — suggested uses include putting it in a potpie (see page 196), tossing with dumplings, serving over potato salad, or glazing with pepper jelly. Printed note (paraphrased): if making the ribs to use the meat in the Short Rib Pot Pie (page 196) or the Short Rib Hash (page 215), let the meat cool completely, cut it off the bone, dice into ¾-inch cubes, and refrigerate until ready to use.
MAKES about 20 cookies | Oven: 375°F convection (400°F regular) | Health Focus: A Treat, in Moderation

Adapted from Poole's.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A treat — best enjoyed occasionally, in a modest portion, rather than as an everyday food
  • Eggs — complete protein with every building block your muscles need to repair, plus choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical and which most people don't get enough of.
  • Dark chocolate — cocoa flavanols help blood vessels relax so blood flows more easily. Darker chocolate means more flavanols and less sugar.
Ingredients
  • 2¼ cups all-purpose flour
  • ¾ teaspoon sea salt
  • 1¼ teaspoons baking soda
  • 1¼ cups unsalted butter
  • 1 cup granulated sugar
  • ½ cup plus 2 tablespoons packed light brown sugar
  • 2 large eggs
  • 1½ teaspoons pure vanilla extract
  • 2½ cups chocolate chips
  • Milk, for serving
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Sift the flour, salt, and baking soda into a medium bowl.
  2. Step 2: In a stand mixer with the paddle attachment, mix the butter and both sugars on medium speed only until barely combined. Add the eggs and vanilla and mix until only partly combined. Add the sifted dry ingredients and mix until the batter is lumpy but not fully combined. Add the chocolate chips and mix until just combined.
  3. Step 3: Using a 2-ounce scoop, scoop the cookies onto a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing them about 2 inches apart. Refrigerate overnight. Freezing option from the page: put the baking sheet in the freezer for 1 hour, then move the cookie rounds to a resealable plastic bag and store in the freezer for up to 6 months.
  4. Step 4: When ready to bake, preheat a convection oven to 375°F (regular oven to 400°F). Bake 12 to 18 minutes, until the edges are golden brown.
  5. Step 5: Cool slightly, then serve with a glass of ice-cold milk.
Intro (paraphrased): a regular dessert at Poole's — warm cookies with a glass of milk; this version aims for crunchy edges with a tender, chewy centre. Two technique points are stressed: mix the dough a bit less than you think you should at each stage (some unincorporated flour in the final dough is fine), and shape, refrigerate overnight, and bake straight from the refrigerator.
Health Focus: Vitamin C

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A drink, not a food — enjoy occasionally; the fresh ingredients are the bright spot
  • Pineapple — vitamin C for immune system and skin, plus bromelain, an enzyme that helps break down protein — why fresh pineapple tenderizes meat and sits well after a heavy meal. Heat destroys the enzyme, so fresh keeps it.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
  • Coconut cream and rum — a dessert in a glass. The pineapple is real fruit; enjoy the whole thing knowingly.
Ingredients
  • 2 OUNCES COCONUT CREAM
  • 2 OUNCES PINEAPPLE JUICE
  • ½ OUNCE FRESH ORANGE JUICE
  • 1 ½ OUNCES YOUR FAVORITE DARK RUM
  • ¾ OUNCE 151 RUM
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a pint glass, combine coconut cream, pineapple juice, orange juice, and rum.
  2. Step 2: Add ice to the mixing glass and shake well.
  3. Step 3: Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice, float a small amount of dark rum on top, and finish with several gratings of fresh nutmeg.
Health Focus: Fresh Herbs & Citrus

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A drink, not a food — enjoy occasionally; the fresh ingredients are the bright spot
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Ginger — its bite comes from gingerol, which helps calm nausea and queasiness and eases everyday inflammation. That's why ginger settles a stomach.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • HALF A HANDFUL OF FRESH MINT
  • 2 LEMON WEDGES
  • 3 LIME WEDGES
  • 2 ½ OUNCES GINGER INFUSED SIMPLE SYRUP
  • 1 ½ OUNCES RUM
  • 1 OUNCE FRESH LEMON JUICE
  • 1 OUNCE FRESH LIME JUICE
  • SODA WATER
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a pint glass, muddle mint with lemon and lime wedges to crush the mint and release citrus juice.
  2. Step 2: Add the simple syrup and muddle a little more; do not strain.
  3. Step 3: Fill the glass with ice.
  4. Step 4: Add rum, lemon juice, and lime juice.
  5. Step 5: Top with soda water, stir, and garnish with extra lemon and lime.
Health Focus: Capsaicin & Metabolism

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Ginger — its bite comes from gingerol, which helps calm nausea and queasiness and eases everyday inflammation. That's why ginger settles a stomach.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
Ingredients
  • 1 CUP SOY SAUCE
  • 1 CUP BROWN SUGAR
  • 2 TABLESPOONS SRIRACHA
  • 1 CUP FRESH ORANGE JUICE
  • 2 JALAPENOS, MINCED
  • 4 CLOVES GARLIC, MINCED
  • 1 3-INCH KNOB GINGER, MINCED
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Put all ingredients together and bring to a strong simmer.
  2. Step 2: Cook 8–10 minutes.
  3. Step 3: If needed, thicken with a corn starch slurry.
Health Focus: Healthy Fats

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Garlic — here it's garlic powder, the dried convenience form: real garlic flavor, though much of fresh garlic's allicin punch is lost in drying.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • ¼ CUP BUTTERMILK
  • ¼ CUP SOUR CREAM
  • ½ CUP MAYONNAISE
  • ½ TEASPOON FRESH PARSLEY, FINELY CHOPPED
  • 1 ¼ TEASPOON FRESH CHIVES, FINELY CHOPPED
  • 1 TEASPOON FRESH DILL, FINELY CHOPPED
  • 2 TABLESPOONS LEMON JUICE
  • ½ TEASPOON ONION POWDER
  • ¼ TEASPOON GARLIC POWDER
  • ½ TEASPOON SALT
  • ¾ TEASPOON BLACK PEPPER
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Mix all ingredients together until smooth.
  2. Step 2: Refrigerate; keeps up to three days.
Health Focus: B Vitamins & Umami

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Mushrooms — deep savory flavor for very few calories, plus B vitamins your body uses to turn food into energy.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
  • Cream soup — the mushrooms are genuinely good food; the cream makes it occasional rather than everyday.
Ingredients
  • ¾ LB. MUSHROOMS
  • A COUPLE ONIONS, CHOPPED
  • 1 TABLESPOON UNSALTED BUTTER
  • 3 TABLESPOONS EVOO
  • 2 TABLESPOONS SHERRY
  • 1 ½ CUPS CHICKEN STOCK
  • ½ CUP HEAVY CREAM
  • 2 TABLESPOONS CHIVES, CHOPPED
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Quarter the mushrooms and chop the onion.
  2. Step 2: In a saucepan over moderate heat, cook mushrooms and onion in butter and olive oil, stirring occasionally, until softened and any liquid given off has evaporated.
  3. Step 3: Add sherry and reduce by half; add chicken stock and cream and simmer 16–18 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Blend half the mixture, then recombine; season with salt and pepper to taste and add more sherry if wanted.
  5. Step 5: Serve garnished with chopped chives.
Garnish with chopped chives.
Health Focus: Lean Protein & Umami

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Mushrooms — deep savory flavor for very few calories, plus B vitamins your body uses to turn food into energy.
  • Ginger — its bite comes from gingerol, which helps calm nausea and queasiness and eases everyday inflammation. That's why ginger settles a stomach.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Peanuts — plant protein plus monounsaturated fat, the heart-friendly kind; the combination keeps you full for a long time.
  • Pork — complete protein for muscles, plus thiamine (vitamin B1), which your body needs to turn food into energy. Tenderloin is the leanest cut of pork — closer to chicken breast than to ribs.
Ingredients
  • 1 PORK TENDERLOIN
  • ¼ CUP RED MISO
  • 4 TABLESPOONS SCALLIONS
  • ⅔ TABLESPOON FRESH GINGER, MINCED
  • ½ CUP PEANUTS, FINELY CHOPPED
  • ⅓ CUP PANKO
  • 3 OUNCES BUTTER, MELTED
  • ⅔ TABLESPOON GRAPESEED OIL
  • SALT AND PEPPER, TO YOUR TASTE
  • FRESH BASIL, CHOPPED
  • FRESH MINT, CHOPPED
  • FRESH CILANTRO, CHOPPED
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a mixing bowl, combine miso, scallions, ginger, peanuts, and panko with the melted butter.
  2. Step 2: Press the mixture onto the pork tenderloin as a crust and refrigerate briefly to set.
  3. Step 3: Heat grapeseed oil in a sauté pan and sear the pork until browned on all sides.
  4. Step 4: Move to a baking sheet and finish in a 375 F oven for 8–9 minutes.
  5. Step 5: Rest, slice on the bias, and garnish with cilantro, basil, and mint. Serve with the Shiitake Scallion Jalapeno Broth below.
