Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Mushrooms — deep savory flavor for very few calories, plus B vitamins your body uses to turn food into energy.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
Ingredients
  • 1 CUP WATER
  • ¼ CUP RED MISO
  • 2 OUNCES SHIITAKE MUSHROOMS, STEMMED AND SLICED
  • 1 JALAPENO PEPPER, SEEDED AND SLICED THINLY
Preparation
  1. Step 1: This is the sub-recipe / broth for Pork Tenderloin with Shiitake Jalapeno Broth (same page).
  2. Step 2: In a saucepan, combine water and miso and heat gently.
  3. Step 3: Add shiitake and jalapeno and let the broth simmer.
none; note scallions appear in the broth title but no scallion quantity is listed in its ingredient list as photographed.
SERVES 4–6 | Oven: 400°F | Health Focus: Allicin & Calcium

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic, roasted — roasting trades allicin (heat destroys it) for sweetness and mellow depth; the health-heavy way to eat garlic is raw or rested, the delicious way is this.
  • Cheese — protein and calcium, which bones are built from, in a small, flavorful amount. It's rich and salty, so here it works as a seasoning, not the main event.
  • Honey — a natural sweetener with trace protective compounds; your body still treats it as sugar, so a little goes a long way.
  • Figs — fiber for digestion, potassium for blood pressure, and natural sweetness, so a little satisfies.
Ingredients
  • 3–4 heads garlic
  • Extra-virgin olive oil
  • Maldon salt
  • Soft, creamy blue cheese with not too much bite, such as Saint Agur or Gorgonzola dolce
  • Fig preserves or runny honey
  • Chewy sourdough baguette
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat oven to 400°F.
  2. Step 2: Remove loose papery outer skins from garlic heads while keeping heads intact; cut tips off each head to expose clove ends.
  3. Step 3: Place foil on a sheet pan, set garlic heads root-side down in the centre, drizzle with oil, sprinkle with salt, and fold foil edges over to form a sealed packet.
  4. Step 4: Bake 40–60 minutes until soft and golden/caramelised.
  5. Step 5: Arrange garlic on a platter/board with the blue cheese and a pot of fig preserves alongside.
  6. Step 6: To eat: spread torn baguette pieces with cheese, squeeze a roasted clove over, and add a small spoonful of preserves; suggested drink pairing is a lightly chilled red or sparkling Lambrusco.
Hot tip (paraphrased): foil-wrapped garlic can instead be cooked over hot coals. Headnote is a short prose passage about favourite autumn smells including roasting garlic.
SERVES 4–6 | Health Focus: Leafy Greens & Protein

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Leafy greens — folate for making new cells and red blood, vitamin K for clotting and bones, and natural nitrates for blood flow, all for almost no calories.
  • Cheese — protein and calcium, which bones are built from, in a small, flavorful amount. It's rich and salty, so here it works as a seasoning, not the main event.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
  • 'Fatty' is honest branding — the greens are the base and the balance; the rich toppings are the flavor, in salad-sized amounts.
Ingredients
  • FOR THE DRESSING
  • 1 cup grapeseed oil
  • 1/3 cup red wine vinegar
  • 3 tablespoons Dijon mustard
  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • 1–2 heads frilly red leaf and/or green leaf lettuce
  • 6–8 petite radishes, thinly shaved and immersed in ice water
  • 4–6 oz Gruyère cheese, grated on the medium holes of a box grater
  • 1 shallot, thinly shaved
  • 1–2 handfuls of herb croutons
  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Make the dressing: blend the oil, vinegar, mustard, 2 pinches of salt and several cracks of pepper until smooth and emulsified, with a creamy, shiny look similar to thick heavy cream. Thin with a little water if needed, taste and adjust; it should be pungent, salty and mustard-forward. Set aside.
  2. Step 2: Trim the lettuce heads and tear the leaves into manageable pieces; place in a large bowl. Drain the radishes, pat dry, and add to the lettuce with half of the Gruyère, the shallot and the croutons. Drizzle dressing over the top and toss gently by hand. Season with salt and plenty of pepper and toss again.
  3. Step 3: Mound the salad high on plates using two hands, finish with the remaining Gruyère and more cracked pepper, and serve immediately.
Headnote (paraphrased) describes a piquant, tangy, rich salad; Batavia lettuce varieties are recommended as the best choice because the loose, frilly leaves have enough body for the emulsified dressing and cheese; use plenty of cheese and black pepper, pile the salad high and dress it with care. Suggested pairing: a floral white or light red wine and a crisp baguette with cold butter. Footer: SOUP & SALAD TIME, page 121.
SERVES 4–6 | Health Focus: Folate & Prebiotic Fiber

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Asparagus — folate for making new cells, plus inulin, a fiber your good gut bacteria feed on (that's what 'prebiotic' means).
  • Cheese — protein and calcium, which bones are built from, in a small, flavorful amount. It's rich and salty, so here it works as a seasoning, not the main event.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
Ingredients
  • 2 bunches asparagus, trimmed of woody ends
  • Wedge of Parmesan cheese (3–4 oz)
  • 8–10 tablespoons butter
  • Maldon salt and freshly ground black pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Blanch the asparagus following the directions on page 18 until tender but still crisp, then shock in an ice bath until cool and drain well.
  2. Step 2: Arrange the asparagus on a serving platter. Grate a generous amount of Parmesan, about 1 cup, over it and let it sit at room temperature while the butter is prepared.
  3. Step 3: Melt the butter in a sauté pan over medium heat. Let it foam, then watch as the milk solids settle and begin to brown; stir occasionally and continue heating until the solids are deep chocolate brown and smell nutty, then take off the heat.
  4. Step 4: Pour the hot brown butter over the platter so it melts the cheese covering the stalks. Sprinkle with salt and several twists of pepper and serve at once with tongs.
Headnote (paraphrased) says the dish was passed down from Uncle Fredo via his mother, in Fredo style, with juicy asparagus coated in Parmesan and brown butter. HOT TIP (paraphrased): Manchego is suggested as an excellent alternative to the Parmesan. Footer: FLAVORS FROM THE FARM.
SERVES 6–8 | Oven: 450°F | Health Focus: Potassium & Resistant Starch

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Potatoes — potassium, which helps keep blood pressure in check by balancing salt, plus filling starch that keeps you full. Much of the fiber is in the skin, so skin-on keeps more of it.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • 4 lb potatoes (see headnote)
  • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil or rendered animal fat
  • Kosher salt
  • 8–10 tablespoons (4–5 oz) butter
  • 6–8 cloves garlic
  • Several fresh thyme, oregano, marjoram, or rosemary sprigs, plus chopped herbs for garnish
  • Splash of dry white wine
  • 3–4 cups bone broth or stock (the best you can find)
  • Maldon salt and freshly ground black pepper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the oven to 450°F.
  2. Step 2: Peel the potatoes and cut them into thick, scallop-like rounds with flattened sides; pat dry. Heat a large, heavy sauté pan over medium heat, add the oil/fat and heat until very hot and slightly smoking; brown in batches if the pan is not large enough.
  3. Step 3: Season the potatoes liberally with kosher salt and place them directly in the hot oil. Leave undisturbed about 5 minutes so a deep sear forms, gently rotating/swirling the pan instead of moving the pieces. When the underside is dark golden brown, flip with a spatula and cook undisturbed until the second side is also dark golden brown.
  4. Step 4: Once both sides are seared, add the butter, garlic cloves and herb sprigs. When the butter melts and foams, cook 1–2 minutes longer. Add the wine to deglaze, stirring to loosen browned bits. Pour in the broth, bring to a boil, transfer the pan to the oven and cook 35–40 minutes, until the potatoes give no resistance when pierced with a knife and the liquid has thickened.
  5. Step 5: Return the pan to the stovetop, move the potatoes to a platter, and reduce the sauce further over medium heat until shiny and emulsified. If it separates, add a little water or oil and bring it back together, then cook 1 more minute.
  6. Step 6: Spoon the sauce over the potatoes, finish with Maldon salt, pepper and chopped herbs, and serve immediately.
Headnote (paraphrased) identifies these as pommes de terre fondantes, described as an easy classic French preparation suitable for a weeknight with roast chicken or displayed around a standing rib roast at New Year's Eve. Butter alone works, but rendered animal fats such as beef tallow, bacon drippings, duck fat or schmaltz are suggested for extra flavour; a gelatinous bone broth or stock is key to the creamy melted texture and emulsified sauce. Waxy potato varieties are said to hold their shape better than starchy russets, though russets can be used; a cast-iron sauté pan is preferred, stainless steel also works; cut sides should be straight rather than sloping to contain liquid and steam. Safety caution (paraphrased): hot fat pops and splatters, so confidence and caution and kitchen goggles or glasses are recommended. Footer: FRIENDS & FAMILY, page 173.
SERVES 12 | Health Focus: Flavanols & Antioxidants

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A treat — best enjoyed occasionally, in a modest portion, rather than as an everyday food
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Eggs — complete protein with every building block your muscles need to repair, plus choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical and which most people don't get enough of.
  • Dark chocolate — cocoa flavanols help blood vessels relax so blood flows more easily. Darker chocolate means more flavanols and less sugar.
  • Honey — a natural sweetener with trace protective compounds; your body still treats it as sugar, so a little goes a long way.
Ingredients
  • 1 lb dark chocolate or blend of dark chocolates, such as TCHO 68% and 99% cacao, chopped
  • 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil, preferably with fruity, buttery notes, plus more for garnish
  • 10 large eggs, chilled
  • 1/4 cup runny honey, for the egg yolks
  • 1/3 cup runny honey, for the egg whites
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a heavy saucepan over low heat, warm the chocolate and oil together, stirring often, until melted and smooth. Set aside to cool slightly.
  2. Step 2: Prepare 2 medium bowls. Separate the eggs one at a time, whites in one bowl and yolks in the other. Add the 1/4 cup honey to the yolks and beat with a handheld electric mixer on medium speed about 10 minutes, until lighter, more buttery in colour and doubled in volume.
  3. Step 3: Clean the beaters very thoroughly so no fatty yolk residue remains. Beat the whites on medium speed until bubbly with a bit of froth.
  4. Step 4: Heat the 1/3 cup honey in a small, heavy pan over medium heat just until it starts to simmer, then remove from the heat. With the mixer on medium speed, stream the hot honey into the whites and beat until they form soft peaks; stiffer whites give a firmer mousse.
  5. Step 5: Stir the yolk mixture briefly to check it has kept its character, then gently stir it into the chocolate–olive oil mixture until evenly coloured.
  6. Step 6: Fold the whipped whites into the chocolate mixture in a few batches, as gently as possible so as not to deflate them, folding just until no white swirls remain.
  7. Step 7: Spoon or pour the mousse into a larger vessel for later portioning, or directly into serving glasses or bowls. Cover the surface tightly with plastic wrap to prevent a skin forming and chill at least overnight or up to 1 day.
Headnote (paraphrased) describes a dairy-free, dense, rich mousse made from farm eggs and honey; portion size can be reduced to make more than twelve servings; it benefits from being made in advance and can be portioned ahead. Because the eggs are raw, the quality of the eggs, chocolate and olive oil is emphasised. Serving suggestions (paraphrased): a glass of Champagne or Château d'Yquem, or a small dollop of crème fraîche or vanilla whipped cream, or fresh raspberries or whole cherries over ice. HOT TIP (paraphrased): just before serving, garnish with a drizzle of the extra-virgin olive oil and a few crystals of Maldon salt. Page 198, footer: FLAVORS FROM THE FARM.
MAKES ONE 9-INCH CAKE | Oven: 325°F if using the convection setting or 400°F if using a conventional oven | Health Focus: Monounsaturated Fats

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • A treat — best enjoyed occasionally, in a modest portion, rather than as an everyday food
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Olive oil instead of butter — the swap trades some saturated fat for the heart-friendlier monounsaturated kind, and keeps the crumb moist for days.
  • Eggs — complete protein with every building block your muscles need to repair, plus choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical and which most people don't get enough of.
Ingredients
  • Butter and all-purpose flour, for the pan
  • 2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
  • 2 1/4 teaspoons kosher salt
  • 1 1/4 teaspoons baking powder
  • 1 teaspoon baking soda
  • 1 1/2 cups sugar
  • 3 large eggs
  • 1 cup plus 2 tablespoons whole milk
  • 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for brushing after baking
  • 1/2 cup fresh orange juice
  • 1 1/4 teaspoon grated orange zest
  • Dash of pure vanilla extract or vanilla bean paste
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the oven to 325°F on convection or 400°F in a conventional oven. Generously grease a 9-inch Bundt pan with butter, getting into every nook, then dust with flour and tap out the excess.
  2. Step 2: In a medium bowl, whisk together the flour, salt, baking powder and baking soda. In a large bowl, combine the sugar, eggs, milk, oil, orange juice and zest, and vanilla and stir to mix well. Fold the flour mixture into the oil mixture just until the batter is evenly moistened and homogeneous.
  3. Step 3: Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Bake 45–60 minutes, until a toothpick inserted into the centre comes out moderately clean.
  4. Step 4: Let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 15 minutes. Brush the top with a good amount of olive oil, unmould the cake onto the rack, lift off the pan, and brush the sides with more oil. Let cool completely before serving.
Headnote (paraphrased) discusses olive oil in sweets in Italy versus newer familiarity in the United States, and says a more intensely flavoured olive oil is better and a fruitier oil is preferred over a peppery one. Serving suggestions (paraphrased): serve plain alongside an afternoon espresso, or dress it up for lunch with softly whipped cream, sugared blueberries, a bit of citrus zest and a dash of Maldon salt, finishing with a drizzle of more olive oil. The cake can be made in advance and is said to taste even better the next day. Footer: SWEETS & TREATS, page 201.
MAKES 6 SERVINGS | Health Focus: Lean Protein & Selenium

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Scallops — lean protein plus B12 for red blood cells and magnesium, a mineral muscles and nerves need to work and relax properly.
  • Pineapple — vitamin C for immune system and skin, plus bromelain, an enzyme that helps break down protein — why fresh pineapple tenderizes meat and sits well after a heavy meal. Heat destroys the enzyme, so fresh keeps it.
  • Honey — a natural sweetener with trace protective compounds; your body still treats it as sugar, so a little goes a long way.
Ingredients
  • 1/2 cup honey mustard
  • 1/4 cup orange marmalade
  • Pinch red pepper flakes (optional)
  • 12 slices bacon,* cut in half crosswise
  • 12 medium sea scallops (8 ounces), cut in half crosswise
  • 1 can pineapple chunks, drained (24 pieces)
  • *Do not use thick-cut bacon.
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Oil the grill grate and prepare the grill for direct cooking over medium heat. Soak 12 (6-inch) bamboo skewers in water for 20 minutes to prevent burning.
  2. Step 2: Stir the mustard, marmalade and red pepper flakes, if using, together in a small bowl. Reserve 1/2 cup of the mustard mixture in a separate small bowl for serving.
  3. Step 3: Wrap one bacon slice around one scallop half and one pineapple chunk and thread onto a skewer. Repeat with the remaining bacon, scallops and pineapple, putting two bacon-wrapped scallops on each skewer.
  4. Step 4: Grill the skewers about 6 minutes, or until the scallops are opaque, turning frequently and brushing with the remaining (non-reserved) mustard mixture. Serve immediately with the reserved mustard mixture.
Section header: Appetizers. Footnote on the bacon: do not use thick-cut bacon.
Health Focus: Homemade over Processed

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Corn, nixtamalized — soaking corn in lime water, the traditional step behind masa, frees its niacin so your body can use it and adds calcium. It's one of the oldest food-processing tricks there is, and it genuinely makes corn more nutritious.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
Ingredients
  • 2 cups corn flour
  • 1 cup water
  • A tortilla press
  • 2 circles of plastic paper
Preparation
  1. Step 1: English "PREPARATION" text, paraphrased: Put the corn flour in a bowl, add the water, and mix softly and quickly to combine. Cover the dough and let it rest 15 minutes.
  2. Step 2: Lightly grease a skillet or comal and heat over medium heat. Place a ball of dough in the tortilla press between the two plastic discs so it does not stick, close the press and press firmly.
  3. Step 3: Open the press, remove the top plastic, and carefully flip the tortilla onto one hand. Remove the remaining plastic and place the tortilla in the skillet/comal. Cook until it begins to lightly brown, then flip it to the first side (called the "face" of the tortilla) and finish cooking; it should puff up slightly. The page also gives the same preparation in Spanish under "PREPARACIÓN".
English subtitle printed: "Handmade Tortillas". Introductory text in Spanish and English (paraphrased) explains the tortilla as food, plate and utensil, dating to the beginnings of agriculture in the Americas, ground/mixed/rolled with stone implements, and describes cooks shaping tortillas with their palms over ceramic or metal comales at feasts and celebrations. Page number 27. The photo at top right shows blocks of a pale solid (masa/cheese-like) — no caption transcribed.
6 porciones / 6 servings | Health Focus: Lean Protein & Vitamin C

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • White fish — lean, complete protein that's easy to digest: the muscle-building basics without any heaviness.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • The lime 'cooks' the fish without heat — acid firms the protein the way heat does, and because there's no cooking, the vitamin C and the fish's delicate fats arrive intact.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • 1 1/2 kg. dorado (mahi mahi or other white fish)
  • 3 large onions, minced
  • 15 limes
  • 15 bitter oranges
  • salt
  • hot chili to taste
  • 3 Tbsp. minced cilantro
  • chili hot sauce (optional)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: English "Preparation" text, paraphrased: Cut the fish into small cubes and place in a glass dish. Add the finely chopped onions and the lime and orange juice. The page's tip is to squeeze the limes and oranges carefully by hand without pressing the peel too hard, so resins that would sour the fish are not released.
  2. Step 2: Add salt and chili to taste, mix with a wooden spoon and cover the bowl. Leave at room temperature for two hours, then refrigerate. Do not marinate too long or the fish will dry out.
  3. Step 3: Just before serving, sprinkle with the minced cilantro. The page also gives the same preparation in Spanish under "Preparación".
English subtitle printed: "Fish Ceviche". A sub-recipe for chili hot sauce appears on the same page (see separate entry below). Page number 55.
Health Focus: Capsaicin

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Carrots and root vegetables — beta-carotene, the orange pigment your body turns into vitamin A for your eyes and immune system. Cooking them and eating them with a little fat helps you absorb far more than raw carrots alone.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Onions and leeks — their fibers are food for the good bacteria in your gut (that's what 'prebiotic' means), and they help calm everyday inflammation.
Ingredients
  • 1 onion, finely minced
  • 1 carrot peeled and minced
  • 12 whole black peppercorns
  • 1 minced Panamanian or jalapeño chili pepper
  • white vinegar
Preparation
  1. Step 1: English "Preparation" text, paraphrased: Put the onion, carrot, peppercorns and chili pepper in a glass jar and cover all the ingredients with enough vinegar. Seal the jar tightly and store for three days so the flavours blend completely. Refrigerate after opening. The Spanish version says to refrigerate once it begins to be used.
none beyond the method above; this is the "salsa picante (opcional)" listed in the ceviche ingredients.
SERVES 4 | Health Focus: Omega-3s & Calcium

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Sardines and anchovies — small fish are the richest easy source of EPA and DHA, the omega-3 fats that help keep heart rhythm steady, calm inflammation, and build brain cells; eating the soft bones adds calcium. Small and short-lived, they also carry far less mercury than big fish.
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
Ingredients
  • 10 fresh whole sardines
  • 10 fresh whole anchovies
  • sea salt flakes and freshly cracked black pepper
  • Lemon thyme oil
  • 500 ml (17 fl oz/2 cups) good-quality extra-virgin olive oil
  • 2 tablespoons lemon thyme leaves or native thyme leaves
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Fillet the sardines: for a right-handed cook, place a sardine with its head to the left off the board, tail to the right and backbone facing you; the fish are filleted with the gut in because removing it beforehand is too time-consuming. Make a small cut behind the head to separate the collar from the rest of the fillet, then cut cleanly down the frame from head to tail to remove the first fillet intact in one movement, letting the bottom fillet rest on the board for support. The second fillet is trickier; use the board for support. No pin-boning is needed, but cut the rib bones out with a small knife.
  2. Step 2: Fillet the remaining sardines and anchovies the same way. Keep the bones, heads and gut, which can be made into garum (see page 73).
  3. Step 3: Make the oil (see also separate Lemon thyme oil entry): preferably in a Thermomix set to 85°C (185°F), blending on high for 10 minutes until fragrant; otherwise bring the oil and thyme leaves to 85°C (185°F) in a small saucepan, then blitz in a blender until fragrant. Strain through a sieve lined with muslin (cheesecloth).
  4. Step 4: To serve, arrange five anchovies on a warmed serving plate and place the sardines on top; repeat with a second plate. Season to taste and pour over enough oil to cover the plates generously. Optional lemon juice can offset the oiliness, but serve with plenty of crusty bread.
Introductory text (paraphrased) stresses using ultra-fresh sardines and anchovies, served warm — not cold — and still raw, not cooked, for texture and flavour, and pairs having both fish on one plate favourably against truffle and foie gras. ALTERNATIVE FISH list at bottom left: Herring; Mackerel. Page 88, section "The Recipes".
Oven: 85°C (185°F) | Health Focus: Herb-Infused Oils

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
Ingredients
  • 500 ml (17 fl oz/2 cups) good-quality extra-virgin olive oil
  • 2 tablespoons lemon thyme leaves or native thyme leaves
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Combine the oil and thyme leaves and heat to 85°C (185°F): in a Thermomix at 85°C (185°F) blend on high for 10 minutes until fragrant, or bring the oil and leaves to that temperature in a small saucepan and then blitz in a blender until fragrant.
  2. Step 2: Strain through a sieve lined with muslin (cheesecloth).
none beyond its use in the main recipe above.
Makes a 3-pound chicken with sauce left over | Health Focus: Anthocyanins & Protein

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Blueberries — their deep-blue color is anthocyanins, protective compounds linked in studies to slower memory decline and healthier blood vessels.
  • Blueberries in a barbecue sauce — their tartness and color do the work bottled sauces give to extra sugar and dye.
  • Chicken — lean, complete protein: all the building blocks for keeping muscle, without much fat, especially with the skin off.
Ingredients
  • 1 3-pound chicken
  • 3 teaspoons salt
  • 1 1/2 teaspoons black pepper
  • Blue Q Sauce
  • 3 cups blueberries
  • 2 cups apple cider vinegar
  • 2 cups granulated sugar
  • 1 3-inch cinnamon stick
  • 1 bay leaf
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 1/4 teaspoon chili flakes
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Cook the chicken: Light the grill and heat it to roughly 350°F. If using charcoal, add some water-soaked cherry-, pecan- or apple-wood chips to the charcoal for a smoke effect.
  2. Step 2: Have the butcher butterfly/spatchcock the chicken by cutting out the backbone and sternum and flattening it. About 10 minutes before cooking, bring the chicken to room temperature and season it thoroughly with 3 teaspoons salt and 1 1/2 teaspoons black pepper.
  3. Step 3: Place the chicken skin-side up on the grill and close the lid. Cook covered for 20 minutes, then begin basting with the blueberry sauce (see Blue Q Sauce entry) every 5 minutes for an additional 20 minutes, keeping the grill lid closed between bastings.
  4. Step 4: After 40 minutes in total, turn the chicken over to caramelise the skin and baste the other side for 10 more minutes. Using a thermometer, check the temperature of a meaty part of the leg; if it is at 165°F, remove it from the grill, otherwise cook until it reaches the proper temperature, skin-side up.
  5. Step 5: Off the grill, douse the chicken in blueberry sauce and let it rest for 10 minutes. Once well rested, cut the chicken into 6 or 8 pieces and toss once more in sauce. Serve warm or at room temperature. The sauce method itself is in the separate Blue Q Sauce entry below.
Introductory text (paraphrased) explains the sauce, called Blue Q, is unlike a traditional Eastern Carolina-style barbecue sauce, is useful on items beyond meat, and works like a shrub — a fruit syrup punctuated by vinegar — mixed with club soda or alcohol, and as a fruity vinaigrette; it is used heavily on the author's own grill menu. Caution (paraphrased): whether using it on chicken or pork, it is not a marinade — brush it on toward the end of cooking and let it soak for a bit before serving, and the final soak is key.
Health Focus: Anthocyanins

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • An accompaniment — a small amount adds a lot of flavor, so a little goes a long way.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
  • Blueberries — their deep-blue color is anthocyanins, protective compounds linked in studies to slower memory decline and healthier blood vessels.
Ingredients
  • Blue Q Sauce
  • 3 cups blueberries
  • 2 cups apple cider vinegar
  • 2 cups granulated sugar
  • 1 3-inch cinnamon stick
  • 1 bay leaf
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 1/4 teaspoon chili flakes
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Combine the blueberries with a little of the vinegar in a food processor and pulse just to break the berries up and get the blue juice flowing, not to make them smooth.
  2. Step 2: In a 4-quart saucepan, combine all the sauce ingredients, bring to a simmer over medium heat and cook, covered, for 1 hour, stirring from time to time because it can burn.
  3. Step 3: Transfer the sauce carefully to a blender, remove the small knob on top of the lid and cover with a dish towel to prevent an explosion, and blend until as smooth as possible. Strain through a fine-mesh strainer back into the saucepan, bring back to a boil and reduce the sauce by a third. It should coat the back of a spoon, with a viscosity more like maple syrup than honey.
  4. Step 4: Refrigerate overnight to let the flavours mellow. The sauce keeps for months, covered, in the refrigerator.
See the Blueberry BBQ Chicken entry above for the headnote uses of this sauce (grilling, shrub-style drink, vinaigrette) and the caution that it is not a marinade.
Serves 4 | Oven: 400°F | Health Focus: Fiber & Carotenoids

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Corn — fiber for digestion, plus lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age.
  • Chicken drippings — the fat is the chicken's own, carrying its flavor into the corn; rich, and a little coats every kernel.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
Ingredients
  • 4 chicken-leg quarters, about 10 ounces each (this means drumettes and thighs attached)
  • 3 teaspoons salt, divided
  • 30 turns of the pepper mill or scant 1 teaspoon black pepper, divided
  • 2 tablespoons vegetable oil
  • 4 cups fresh corn
  • 1 teaspoon granulated sugar
  • 4 thyme sprigs
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the oven to 400°F. Season both sides of the chicken with 2 teaspoons of the salt and 10 turns of the pepper mill.
  2. Step 2: In a 12-inch skillet, heat the vegetable oil over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the chicken skin-side down and let it begin to brown slowly, without the oil smoking — the sound should be a gentle rendering of fat and caramelising of skin.
  3. Step 3: As the legs brown, toss the corn with the remaining salt, black pepper and the sugar. Spread it on a 13x18-inch baking sheet with no more than a 1-inch lip, reaching to the edges in a 1/2-inch layer. Lay the 4 thyme sprigs on top of the corn to mark where the chicken will be placed.
  4. Step 4: Once the skin side of the legs is golden brown, lay the chicken skin-side up on top of each thyme sprig, with an inch or two between the legs. Slide the sheet pan onto the middle rack of the oven and roast for 45 minutes.
  5. Step 5: On removing it from the oven, the corn should be cooked unevenly across the pan: the edges dry and caramelised and the corn under the chicken juicy and fragrant. Remove the leg quarters, set them aside and discard the thyme. Stir all the corn together with a spoon or spatula and serve it under the chicken.
Headnote (paraphrased) recounts that the dish recreates corn roasted under a chicken as made by the author's grandmother Iris, as described by his aunt Currie — savoury, caramelised, chewy in places, creamy in others and spicy with black pepper — and notes the method goes against what the author considers "correct" cooking technique. The pan, temperature and size of the chicken legs are said to matter very much. Running heads: page 222, DEEP RUN ROOTS; page 223, SWEET CORN.
Serves 6 | Health Focus: Lean Protein & Hydration

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Crab — lean protein, plus zinc for your immune system and B12 for red blood cells and energy.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
  • Cucumber — mostly water, so it hydrates and fills with almost no calories, plus a little vitamin K for bones and clotting.
  • Cheese — protein and calcium, which bones are built from, in a small, flavorful amount. It's rich and salty, so here it works as a seasoning, not the main event.
  • Fresh herbs — big flavor from leaves full of protective plant compounds, so the dish needs less salt to taste seasoned. Tender herbs go in near the end: long heat dulls the flavor and the benefit together.
Ingredients
  • 2 medium cucumbers or 1 large English cucumber
  • 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, divided
  • 1 cup cream cheese, at room temperature
  • 1 tablespoon Greek yogurt, sour cream, or crème fraîche
  • 1 pound picked crabmeat (anything but claw will work fine)
  • 1/4 cup lemon juice
  • 2 tablespoons prepared horseradish
  • 1/2 teaspoon hot sauce
  • 1/4 cup finely chopped scallion
  • 3 tablespoons chopped mint
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Peel, halve and seed 1 1/2 medium cucumbers or 2/3 of a large English cucumber. Using a mandoline, slice the halves into 1/16-inch half-moons. Toss the slices with 1/2 teaspoon salt and set them over a colander to drain while the rest of the dip is made; this should yield roughly 1 cup of limp cucumber slices.
  2. Step 2: Using a Microplane, grate the remaining cucumber; this leaves cucumber pulp and the water that leaches from it. Strain the pulp from the water and discard the pulp. Set aside up to 1/3 cup of the water for the dip (the text jokes the remainder can be drunk as-is or with tequila).
  3. Step 3: In the bowl of a mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, beat the cream cheese, yogurt and cucumber water until lightened and smooth. Add the crab, the remaining salt, lemon juice, horseradish, hot sauce, scallion and mint, and paddle until it looks like dip.
  4. Step 4: Stir in the cucumber slices by hand and serve chilled with crackers, crudités or chips.
Headnote (paraphrased) credits the author's friend Eleanor Johnston and family gatherings built around dips, notes the author's family dislikes mayonnaise, and explains the cucumber was paired with crab (inspired by a note in Gray Kunz's The Elements of Taste that hands smell like cucumber after handling crab) to add freshness and texture, giving a lighter, "wetter" crab dip. Serving suggestion (paraphrased): plain Jane salt-seasoned crackers and a crisp cool glass of white wine. Running head: page 251, CUCUMBERS.
Serves 2 | Health Focus: Gingerols & Complete Protein

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Eggs — complete protein with every building block your muscles need to repair, plus choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical and which most people don't get enough of.
  • Mushrooms — deep savory flavor for very few calories, plus B vitamins your body uses to turn food into energy.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Ginger — its bite comes from gingerol, which helps calm nausea and queasiness and eases everyday inflammation. That's why ginger settles a stomach.
Ingredients
  • ½ cup long-grain rice
  • 3 tablespoons butter, divided
  • 1 tablespoon vegetable oil
  • 1 cup diced shiitake mushrooms (you can substitute any mushroom you like)
  • 1 heaping tablespoon minced ginger
  • 1 teaspoon minced garlic
  • 1 cup leeks, white part only, sliced ¼ inch thick
  • ¼ teaspoon chili flakes
  • 1 teaspoon salt, divided
  • 2 large eggs
  • 2 tablespoons picked cilantro
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Cook the rice following the instructions on page 292, then let it sit uncovered in the refrigerator a minimum of 1 hour and up to overnight, so it dries slightly and will crisp better.
  2. Step 2: In a 10- to 12-inch sauté pan heat 1 tablespoon butter and the vegetable oil over medium heat until foaming. Add shiitakes, shake pan once, leave undisturbed and let caramelize 2 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Add 1 tablespoon butter, then the cooked rice. Press rice into a thin layer covering the whole pan surface. Once pressed, leave it alone and resist stirring. Add garlic, leeks, chili flakes and ½ teaspoon salt on top.
  4. Step 4: After about 3 minutes, lift a little rice at the edge with a spatula to check: once it has started to take on slight golden colour and crisp texture, stir in the ingredients that were sitting on top, press rice down again into an even layer, and cook another 2 minutes before removing from heat.
  5. Step 5: Cook the eggs and serve: In a 10-inch cast-iron skillet (or preferred egg pan) heat the remaining butter over medium heat until foaming. Crack eggs onto opposite sides of the pan and cook gently about 2 minutes, until whites are set. Sprinkle eggs with remaining ½ teaspoon salt.
  6. Step 6: Fluff the rice and serve it topped with a runny fried egg; garnish with cilantro.
Intro frames this as a way to turn leftover rice into a new dish; almost any ingredients on hand can be used, but success depends on letting the rice sit undisturbed in the hot fat and not stirring it.
Serves 2 | Health Focus: Fiber & Mucilage

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Corn — fiber for digestion, plus lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age.
  • Okra — its slippery soluble fiber slows how fast sugar from a meal reaches your blood, and gives gut bacteria something to feed on.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
  • Fried — but okra's fiber survives the pan, which is more than most fried food offers.
Ingredients
  • ½ cup cornmeal
  • 1 teaspoon salt, divided
  • ¼ teaspoon cayenne
  • 2 cups of okra sliced ⅓ inch thick (about 15 medium okra)
  • cup vegetable oil
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Stir cornmeal, ½ teaspoon salt and cayenne together in a medium bowl. Rinse okra well, toss the damp okra with the cornmeal mixture, and set aside.
  2. Step 2: In a 12-inch cast-iron skillet heat the oil over medium-high heat. When oil shimmers, test with one piece of okra; if it sizzles right away, add all the remaining okra, spreading it in a single layer so every piece touches oil.
  3. Step 3: Lower heat slightly and cook undisturbed on one side 4 minutes.
  4. Step 4: Toss okra with a spatula and cook a further 3 to 4 minutes, until pieces range from honey-brown to chestnut to blond.
  5. Step 5: Lift out with a slotted spoon onto a paper-towel-lined plate to drain. Season with remaining ½ teaspoon salt and serve warm.
Intro explains the dish combines different fried-okra styles the author encountered; despite the name given, it is served draining on a paper-towel-lined plate.
Incomplete as photographed: oil quantity fraction is partly cropped/blurred at the right edge of the ingredient column; best reading is ⅓ cup. All other ingredients and the full method are legible.
Makes 6–8 servings | Oven: 400°F | Health Focus: Whole Grains

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Eggs — complete protein with every building block your muscles need to repair, plus choline, which your brain uses to make a key memory-and-focus chemical and which most people don't get enough of.
  • Corn — fiber for digestion, plus lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age.
Ingredients
  • 1/2 cup (4 oz) salted butter, melted, plus 1 tablespoon for the skillet
  • 1/4 cup avocado or canola oil
  • 2 large eggs
  • 2 cups buttermilk
  • 1 cup fine-grind heirloom yellow cornmeal
  • 1 cup all-purpose flour
  • 3/4 cup organic sugar
  • 1 tablespoon baking powder
  • 1 teaspoon kosher salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat oven to 400°F.
  2. Step 2: In a liquid measuring cup, combine melted butter and oil. In a medium bowl, whisk eggs and buttermilk until smooth. In a large bowl, whisk cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt. Add buttermilk-egg mixture to cornmeal mixture and whisk together. Stream in butter-oil mixture while whisking constantly until smooth.
  3. Step 3: Preheat a 10- to 12-inch cast-iron skillet over medium heat for 2 minutes. Add the 1 tablespoon butter; when melted, pour in batter and cook 1 minute to create the crust.
  4. Step 4: Transfer skillet to oven and bake until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean, 25–30 minutes; timing can vary (as fast as 20 minutes and as slow as 40 minutes depending on skillet size and oven).
  5. Step 5: Place skillet on a trivet and let corn bread rest and relax at room temperature for 30 minutes before cutting.
Intro notes starting in a hot buttered cast-iron skillet creates a rich, crispy toffee-like crust; recipe is intentionally rich like yellow birthday cake in butter/eggs/sugar; suggested treats: with butter and honey, or with a scoop of vanilla ice cream and fresh-picked lavender.
Makes 4 servings | Health Focus: Calcium & Whole Grains

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Cheese — protein and calcium, which bones are built from, in a small, flavorful amount. It's rich and salty, so here it works as a seasoning, not the main event.
  • Made from scratch — whole ingredients you can name, so you know exactly what's in it: no preservatives, and no hidden sugars or oils you didn't choose.
Ingredients
  • 4–6 cups organic whole milk
  • 1 1/2 cups coarse-ground heirloom grits
  • 4 tablespoons salted butter, cut into cubes and kept cold
  • 2 cups grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese
  • 1 tablespoon freshly ground black pepper
  • Kosher salt
Preparation
  1. Step 1: First determine the grain-to-liquid ratio and total cook time for the grits being used from the package / mill / farm instructions, noting some coarse grits need overnight soaking before cooking tender.
  2. Step 2: General method: In a large saucepan over medium heat, bring 4 cups of the milk to a gentle simmer. Slowly stream in grits while whisking constantly.
  3. Step 3: Cook grits for the time indicated on the package instructions, whisking frequently; if needed, continue adding milk 1/2 cup at a time until cooked to desired doneness.
  4. Step 4: Whisk in butter a few cubes at a time, then whisk in cheese and finally pepper.
  5. Step 5: Season with salt to liking and serve immediately.
Intro explains cacio e pepe is a Roman pasta dish of grated aged hard cheese and freshly ground black pepper, originally shepherds' food; applied to grits it makes a bold, creamy bowl. Recommendation to follow the suggested method of the mill or farm the grits are sourced from; instructions often available online if not on package.
SERVES 6 | Health Focus: Potassium & Healthy Fats

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Potatoes — potassium, which helps keep blood pressure in check by balancing salt, plus filling starch that keeps you full. Much of the fiber is in the skin, so skin-on keeps more of it.
  • Avocado — creamy from monounsaturated fat, the kind that supports a healthier cholesterol balance, plus plenty of potassium for blood pressure.
  • Citrus — vitamin C, which your body uses to build collagen for skin and joints and to help fight off illness. It also helps you absorb the iron in plant foods like beans and greens, so a squeeze over them does real work. Vitamin C breaks down in heat, so citrus added at the end keeps more.
Ingredients
  • 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil
  • 1 cup sliced leeks (split the leeks lengthwise first and cut into ¼-inch-thick slices)
  • ½ cup finely chopped Spanish onion
  • 3 garlic cloves, crushed and peeled
  • Sea or kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • 4 cups ½-inch-dice russet (baking) potatoes
  • 2 cups chicken stock or canned low-sodium broth
  • 2 cups water
  • 1 tablespoon fresh thyme leaves
  • 2 teaspoons dried oregano
  • ¾ cup heavy cream
  • GARNISHES
  • ¾ cup heavy cream
  • 2 ripe avocados
  • Generous splash of lemon juice
  • Sea or kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • 3 tablespoons drained capers
  • 2 tablespoons fresh dill
  • 2 tablespoons chopped fresh chives
  • 2 teaspoons fresh lemon thyme leaves
  • 2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil
  • 3 lemons, cut in half
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Heat the olive oil in a pot. Add the leeks, onion, and garlic and cook until translucent.
  2. Step 2: Season with salt and pepper, then add the potatoes.
  3. Step 3: Pour in the chicken stock and water, add the thyme and oregano, and cook the potatoes until tender.
  4. Step 4: Meanwhile, put the garnish cream in the refrigerator to chill. Slice the avocados and toss them with the lemon juice.
  5. Step 5: Blend the soup with an immersion blender (or a regular blender) until smooth and creamy — the potato cream. Thin with a little water or stock if needed.
  6. Step 6: Ladle the potato cream into serving bowls. Top with the chilled cream, the avocado slices, capers, and the herbs (dill, chives, and lemon thyme), drizzle with the olive oil, and serve with the lemon halves.
Intro (paraphrased): inspired by ajiaco, a Colombian potato and chicken stew with herbs and avocado served in Queens, New York; this version leaves out the chicken to make a side dish that goes with many entrées, such as chicken or lightly smoked cod.
Method note: the method is on the facing page (page 30), which appears only as cut-off line beginnings at the right edge of the dish photo. The steps above are rebuilt from every legible fragment of that page — the start of each printed line — together with the ingredient list on page 29. The ends of the lines are cut off in the photo and could not be read, so any exact cooking times in the original are not stated here.
SERVES 2 | Oven: 375°F [190°C] | Health Focus: Calcium & Protein

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Tomatoes — lycopene, the red pigment, helps protect the heart and blood vessels, and cooking tomatoes in a little oil makes it much easier for your body to absorb: one case where cooked beats raw.
  • Pineapple — vitamin C for immune system and skin, plus bromelain, an enzyme that helps break down protein — why fresh pineapple tenderizes meat and sits well after a heavy meal. Heat destroys the enzyme, so fresh keeps it.
  • Cheese — protein and calcium, which bones are built from, in a small, flavorful amount. It's rich and salty, so here it works as a seasoning, not the main event.
  • A grilled cheese is a grilled cheese — the pineapple and tomato lighten it and add real nutrients, but rich and salty is the honest headline.
Ingredients
  • 4 slices fresh pineapple (about ¼ in [6 mm] thick), cored, or ½ of a small can of pineapple rings in juice, drained
  • 6 to 8 slices ripe plum tomato (about ¼ in [6 mm] thick)
  • 1 Tbsp salted butter, at room temperature
  • 4 slices Hawaiian bread (slightly sweet white bread) or artisan white bread
  • 4 slices [85 g] fontina cheese
  • 4 oz [115 g] sliced ham
  • 3 oz [85 g] fresh mozzarella cheese, thinly sliced
  • Pinch of red pepper flakes (optional)
Preparation
  1. Step 1: Preheat the oven to 375°F [190°C] and line a baking sheet with parchment paper or aluminium foil.
  2. Step 2: Lay the pineapple and tomato slices on the prepared sheet and bake 12 minutes, until the surfaces look dry but not yet browned, turning the pieces over halfway through. Remove from the oven and set aside.
  3. Step 3: Heat a cast-iron or nonstick skillet over medium-low heat.
  4. Step 4: Butter one side of each bread slice, dividing the butter evenly. Put two slices buttered-side down on a clean cutting board. On each, layer two slices of the fontina, half of the ham, three or four slices of the roasted tomato, two rings of the roasted pineapple, and half of the mozzarella. Sprinkle with the red pepper flakes if using. Top with the remaining bread slices, buttered-side up.
  5. Step 5: With a wide spatula, put both sandwiches in the pan, cover, and cook until the bottoms are nicely browned, about 4 minutes. Turn and cook until the second sides are browned, the cheese is melted, and the fillings are heated through, about 4 minutes longer.
  6. Step 6: Cut the sandwiches in half if desired and serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): based on the authors' fondness for Hawaiian pizza — mozzarella, sweet-tart pineapple, savoury ham, and spicy tomato sauce — turned into a grilled cheese sandwich using fresh, high-quality ingredients.
SERVES 6 AS A SIDE DISH | Health Focus: Fiber & Carotenoids

Adapted from a cookbook.

Why It's Healthy:

  • Olive oil — mostly monounsaturated fat, the kind that helps keep cholesterol in a healthier balance, plus bitter plant compounds that protect blood vessels. Gentle heat keeps the most of it; the best oil is worth saving for finishing.
  • Garlic — crushing or chopping garlic creates allicin, the compound that helps keep blood vessels flexible and supports your immune system. To keep the most of it: crush or mince it, let it sit about 10 minutes so the allicin can form, then cook gently or add it near the end — hard heat destroys it fast.
  • Corn — fiber for digestion, plus lutein, a yellow pigment that collects in your eyes and helps protect your vision as you age.
  • Potatoes — potassium, which helps keep blood pressure in check by balancing salt, plus filling starch that keeps you full. Much of the fiber is in the skin, so skin-on keeps more of it.
  • Chiles and peppers — capsaicin, the heat compound, warms you up and opens blood flow a little; the peppers bring a lot of vitamin C for your immune system and skin. Vitamin C fades with long cooking, so peppers kept crisp or lightly cooked keep more.
Ingredients
  • 1 Tbsp salted butter
  • 1½ tsp olive oil
  • 1 medium yellow onion, cut into ¼-in [6-mm] dice
  • 1 large garlic clove, minced
  • 1 tsp minced fresh thyme or ½ tsp dried thyme
  • 1 Tbsp plus 2 tsp all-purpose flour
  • 3 cups [720 ml] vegetable stock
  • ¾ cup [180 ml] heavy cream
  • 2 medium Yukon gold potatoes, peeled and cut into ¼-in [6-mm] dice
  • Kernels from 3 ears fresh corn or 2 cups [340 g] frozen corn kernels, drained
  • ¾ tsp piment d'Espelette chile powder or cayenne pepper
  • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
  • 1 Tbsp minced fresh flat-leaf parsley
Preparation
  1. Step 1: In a medium soup pot over medium heat, melt the butter in the olive oil. Add the onion and cook, stirring often, until translucent, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and thyme and cook 1 minute longer.
  2. Step 2: Sprinkle the flour into the onion mixture gradually, whisking constantly to avoid lumps. Stir in the vegetable stock and raise the heat to bring it to a low boil. Add the cream and potatoes and return to a boil. Lower the heat to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the potatoes can be easily pierced with a fork, about 7 minutes.
  3. Step 3: Stir in the corn and the piment d'Espelette, and season with salt and pepper. Simmer, stirring occasionally, until the corn is tender, about 10 minutes longer. Take off the heat and stir in the parsley.
  4. Step 4: Ladle the chowder into bowls and serve immediately.
Intro (paraphrased): a popular summer special — the kitchen goes through about fifty ears of just-picked corn a day; the sweet corn comes through the cream and herbs, the potatoes add body, and a pinch of chile powder cuts the richness. Serving suggestion: serve with a salad made with ripe, fresh heirloom tomatoes. Technique note (paraphrased): to cut kernels from a fresh cob, cut the cob in half crosswise, stand each half up on its thicker end on a clean cutting board, and carefully run a sharp knife down all sides of the standing cob.

What each recipe covers — and what it doesn't

Every recipe now shows estimated nutrition per serving, scored 0–5 against your daily target, with the exact % alongside. By default the target is the FDA Daily Values (2,000 kcal reference) — enter your details below to personalize it. Pick the recipes you're eating below \u2014 and how many servings of each \u2014 to see the combined intake — what the meal covers for the day, and what it doesn't.

How to read the scores: 0–5 dots per nutrient — 0 is under 5% of your daily target, 1 is 5–19%, 2 is 20–49%, 3 is 50–79%, 4 is 80–119%, 5 is 120% or more. The exact % sits next to the dots. For sodium, saturated fat and cholesterol the target is a daily limit — more dots means closer to the limit, not better.

Your daily targets

By default, scores use FDA Daily Values (2,000 kcal). Enter your details for targets matched to you — saved only in your browser, never sent anywhere.

Height is needed for the most accurate calorie estimate (Mifflin-St Jeor). Leave it blank for a rougher weight-only estimate — the page will say so.

Using FDA Daily Values (2,000 kcal reference).

How your targets are calculated

Calories: basal metabolic rate (BMR) by Mifflin-St Jeor — men: 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age + 5; women: the same, minus 161 (Mifflin et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 1990) — multiplied by an activity factor: sedentary 1.2, lightly active 1.375, moderately active 1.55, very active 1.725, extra active 1.9. Without height, BMR is estimated from weight alone (24 kcal/kg/day (10.9 kcal/lb/day) for men, 22 (10.0 kcal/lb/day) for women) and labelled as a rough estimate. Protein: 1.2–1.6 g per kg of body weight per day (0.55–0.73 g/lb) (Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030), scaled by activity from 1.2 (sedentary) to 1.6 (very/extra active). Fat: 20–35% of calories and carbohydrate: 45–65% (acceptable ranges, Dietary Guidelines); the dots use the middle of each range. Fiber: about 14 g per 1,000 kcal. Iron, calcium, vitamin D, vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium use age- and sex-specific recommended intakes (NIH Office of Dietary Supplements); sodium (2,300 mg), saturated fat (under 10% of calories) and cholesterol (300 mg) are daily limits. Total sugars has no daily value. Targets are estimates for a generally healthy adult, not medical advice.

Select one or more recipes to see the combined intake for one serving of each.

Builds on Pairs well with: one tap drafts a full day of eating from the archive — recipes and portion sizes chosen to get every nutrient as close to 5 dots as the archive allows, scored with the same daily targets as the combiner above. Sauces and cocktails are never meal components; a dessert appears only as a small treat, if at all. Plans keep to two or three dishes: a real breakfast, then one main dish cooked once and eaten for both lunch and dinner, with portion sizes — not extra cooking — doing the rest of the work. Nothing is applied until you say so, and the manual combiner stays exactly as it is.

All values are estimates from USDA FoodData Central data — not laboratory analysis. Where an ingredient has no USDA entry it is left out and noted on the recipe; where a recipe doesn't state a quantity, standard amounts are assumed and noted. Salt to taste is not counted, so sodium may be higher.
